On the motion of Hon. S. F. Tolmie (Minister of Agriculture) Bill. No. 78, to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, was read a second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

What change does this
Bill make?

Under the old Act a person could collect two-thirds of the compensation based on the valuation of the animal in its healthy condition, and in addition could secure any salvage that might be derived from the carcass in the event of the flesh upon the animal being slaughtered passing as fit for food. As an example, in the case of a pure bred cow worth $150, two-thirds of her valuation would be $100. We will presume that she would dress six hundred pounds of beef which in an inspected abbatoir would pass as fit for food, being only slightly affected. That carcass would bring about twenty cents per pound for cow beef and yield $120, making a total of $220, or $70 [DOT]more than the animal was worth when she was alive had she passed the tuberculin test. The Bill proposes to do away with that sale and permit the payment of the compensation Only.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

On motion of Hon. Mr. Tolmie consideration was resumed in committee from April 28 of the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Resolved, that It is expedient to amend the Oleomargarine Act, 1919, Chapter twenty-four of the Statutes of 1919, second session, and to provide:
1.	That section three of the said Act be amended so as to extend the time during which the manufacture in and importation of oleomargarine into Canada is permitted until the thirty-first day of August, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one, and to extend the time during which the offering for sale, the sale, and the having in possession for sale of oleomargarine is permitted until the first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two.
2.	That section eight of the said Act be amended to provide that the Governor in Council may make regulations with respect to the importation, manufacture, inspection, marking, advertising and sale of oleomargarine, and the seizure and confiscation of apparatus and materials used, or intended to be used, in the manufacture, treatment, or manipulation of oleomargarine in contravention of the said Act or of any regulation thereunder; and that such regulations may prescribe a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars recoverable upon summary conviction for the violation of any regulation made under the provisions of the said section.
3.	That section nine of the said Act be amended to provide that the penalty for violation of the provisions of the said section shall be enforcible Upon summary conviction, and further that in no case shall the minimum penalty be less than fifty dollars.

Mr. DONALD SUTHERLAND (South Oxford); Before the resolution is passed I would like to make a few observations thereon. The resolution confirms the old adage, " that water, never rises above its source," and I think I might add, "nor a government above the people." The situation at present demands something more than merely temporary remedies. There are quite a number of medical men in the House, and I think they will agree with me not only that desperate diseases require heroic remedies but that, merely prescribing temporary palliatives does not overcome a disease nor remove the root of the trouble.
This oleomargarine question came before Parliament in 1917. For many years previously strong efforts had been made by those who were interested or desired to be interested, in the manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada, to acquire the right to manufacture the commodity in this country and also import it, but down to October 25, 1917, nothing was done in that regard by the Canadian Government. It was after the coming into office of the present Administration that action along the line referred to was taken not by Parliament, but by the Order in Council; granting permission to import oleomargarine and also to manufacture it in the Dominion. The reason assigned for this proceeding was that it was a temporary war measure, and that the existing situation demanded that something of the kind should be done. In 1919- after a further extension of time had been granted and the war had been over for a year-an Act was introduced into Parliament and passed permitting the importation into and the manufacture of this commodity in Canada. The United States experience in regard to oleomargarine-where its manufacture had been permitted, I believe, since IDOL-was. such as to put the people of Canada on their guard as to the difficulties which would be encountered once the manufacture of the article was permitted in this country. I want it distinctly understood at the outset that I have never opposed the importation of oleomargarine into Canada or its manufacture here; but I have opposed, and consistently opposed-the privilege granted to manufacturers and importers to manufacture and bring into Canada, an article mixed with one of our most important dairy products. When the Bill referred to was introduced I objected as strongly as I could to the regulations which had been passed by the Government granting this privilege, and that is the stand I take to-day. If oleomargarine has the virtues which its advocates

claim for it, it can stand on its own merits, and it has nothing to fear. In my opinion there is no justification for permitting the manufacturers of this article of food the sole right to mix butter with it. It is well known that the dairy product represents about forty percent of the component parts of the best margarine, about fifteen per cent being absorbed from the milk in which it is churned in milk and treated with a culture in order to give the manufactured article a butter flavour, the other twenty-five per cent being pure butter. At the beginning of November of last year I understand that the manufacturers had between 6,000,000 and 7,000,000 pounds of butter in storage with a view to incorporating it in their margarine. '
Now, so far as my constituency is concerned, I am not very much interested in this matter, although I come from what has always been known as the first county in this country to establish the dairy industry on a commercial basis, the first cheese factory in Canada having been established there in 1864. The name "Ingersoll" as connected with the dairy industry is well known not only in this country but in Great Britain, and Ingersoll cheese has achieved a world reputation second to none. At the present time I do not know of a single creamery in my constituency that will be manufacturing butter, nor a single cheese factory that will be manufacturing cheese this year. Yet in the face of that condition of affairs it is claimed that the manufacture and importation of margarine is not going to injure the dairy industry, but is designed solely to place within the reach of the poor that essential element in their diet which otherwise they could not hope to purchase. But I believe that many of our farmers to-day are competing with the people in the towns and cities in the purchase of butter for their own tables. Consequently I cannot be accused of acting in the interests of the farmers of my constituency, for as a matter of fact they are very largely consumers rather than producers of butter.
But I do want to warn hon. members and the people of this country that not by encouraging the manufacture and importation of margarine are we going to overcome the difficulties which confront us at the present time. Those difficulties will be overcome only when our people begin to realize that hard labour devoted to food production is in the final analysis the enly proper method of dealing with this question.
Our butter has won an enviable reputation in the Old Country. Ontario is the
second largest producer of butter among our provinces. The province of Quebec, where the conditions are admirably adapted to the production of butter, is by long odds our greatest producer at the present tijne, and the quality of the butter turned out by the creameries of that province is very high indeed, and as a result their butter has won a well-deserved reputation. Yet 1 notice that not later than January last, under the administration of the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie), the dairying industry in this country, which represents an investment of hundreds of millions of dollars, is to be used as the basis to build up a great manufacturing industry devoted to the production of oleomargarine. That is the very object sought by those who are agitating for this extension of the time for the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine.
It may be said that urgent representations have been made to the Government by boards of trade and other representative bodies in favour of these concessions being granted. I admit that such is the case, but it will be found that those representations owe their origin largely to those interested in the manufacture of margarine. We hear a great deal about the big interests and the methods they adopt. -I doubt whether, in the experience of the oldest member of this House anything has occurred similar to the incident that took place in this House a week ago. I was sponsor for a resolution, and urged very strongly in this House the granting of the franchise to our women, and I am very happy to state that they to-day are on a political equality with the men. What I have reference to is a magazine which was placed on the desks of this Chamber the other day, and which I called attention to at the time. I understand a young woman was sent from Toronto with a bundle of these magazines to distribute here. Let me draw attention to the heading that adorns this full page article, which is, I have no doubt, a paid advertisement issued by the people who are interested in the manufacture of oleomargarine. This is the form:
To the Members of the Dominion Parliament.
Prom the Executive of the National Council of Women.
Do you want our vote? Tens of thousands ot women insist that they shall continue to have margarine for use in their households, and they will not vote for the men who oppose it.
I can scarcely believe that our big, strong, rugged-looking Minister of Agriculture would submit to a threat of that kind. I think the pressure must have been from an

entirely different source- possibly in the form of moral suasion rather than a threat.
Now, hon. members may have noticed that for some time a very active propaganda has been carried on among certain associations in the city of Ottawa, for the continuance of the importation and manufacture of margarine. I have been a fairly consistent advocate of protection for our industries, for I have a distinct recollection of the campaign that was carried on in 1878 when conditions were not very satisfactory here. After the abrogation of the (Reciprocity Treaty with the United States, our people found themselves in a very awkward and difficult situation, but they extricated themselves by developing channels of trade, not north and south, but east and west; and by pursuing a system of railway construction unequalled in the history of the world, we have achieved economic independence. I have been a fairly consistent advocate of that policy. In 1911 when a tariff issue was before the people I entered into that campaign, possibly at as great a sacrifice as any member of the House, with a strong feeling that the measure proposed was not in the interests of the country. I am therefore at a loss to understand why the people engaged in this great industry should be singled out and forced to compete with industries of other countries under very unfair conditions. The member for Frohtenac (Mr. Edwards) made reference to this phase of the question when he spoke the other night. One thing is certain: you may by legislation force the farmers out of the dairy business. The people engaged in the dairy industry may not be an organized body and, consequently, may not be able to force acceptance of their views or to protect their interests as other organized bodies do. But in the final analysis you will have to reckon with them if they are to be singled out in this way.
Butter enjoys a protective tariff of four cents a pound; yet you permit the free importation into this country of an article which may contain thirty per cent of butter,
I and that article comes into competition with the product of the dairy industry. The same thing applies to all the ingredients that go to make up this compound. Now, let us be consistent. If the dairy industry is such a valuable one for this country, it should be conducted and built up under the same conditions which have assisted in the building up of other industries. I am not so sure that one of the objects in the mind of those who first in-
£Mr. Sutherland.]
troduced the free importation and manufacture of oleomargarine was not to show what could be done under free trade in the building up of a great industry. Perhaps they wanted to be able to point to the fact that in Toronto, where American concerns have secured control of the stock-yards, two magnificent industries have been built up without a protective tariff, industries which are turning out this article of food by the millions of pounds. I admit that they did it without any tariff. But under Order in Council they have been enabled to utilize the dairy industry of this country to build up that new industry; they have obtained the exclusive right to mix butter with the ingredients that go to make up this margarine. The Dairy Industry Act of 1914 provides the most stringent regulations with regard to the dairy industry and imposes severe penalties upon those who violate its conditions. When you turn to the regulations, what do you find? By Order in Council these people are permitted to go into the markets, purchase millions of pounds of butter, mix it with the other ingredients which enter into the manufacture of margarine, and colour the product to suit the market. Not only that, the regulations provide that margarine shall be sold in half-pound and pound packages. Butter has been sold in this way for many years. Why were these conditions embodied in the regulations? Did the manufacturers of oleomargarine draft them and submit them to the Government for approval? They certainly could not be more carefully drafted in the interests of these people than they are.
In the United States, where enormous quantities of this article are manufactured, an internal revenue tax of ten cents is imposed on every pound which is manufactured, if it contains any colouring matter, and a tax of one-quarter of a cent per pound if it does not contain any colouring. That was found necessary because of the frauds that had been perpetrated; the manner in which the law was being evaded simply amounted to a scandal. Well, why should there be any difference between the coloured article and the uncoloured article? One would surely contain as much nutrition as the other, and there should not be any serious objection, one would think, to the colouring. But butter has obtained a standing that has not come about during recent years. Four thousand years ago butter was a well known commodity, among the Hindus, and from that time down to

the present it has been a staple article oi food throughout the world. It is well known that milk fat contains a substance that was put there by an all-wise Creator for the nourishment and building up and development of the young. If you deprive young and growing children of this fat substance they will not attain strong and healthy development. At John Hopkins university numerous tests along that line have been carried out by Dr. E. V. McCal-lum; it has been proved that no young animal can be satisfactorily developed and brought to maturity unless it is given the fat which is contained in milk. It is asserted that this margarine contains food qualities and that it is in the interests of the young that it should be sold to the people. But those who have investigated the matter agree that no substitute for butter has so far been found which will supply the needs of the young. Oleomargarine may be tolerated for those who have attained maturity; the fat contained in it may sustain such persons, although I think that even that matter is open to question.
In 1919 certain sworn evidence in connection with the cost of living was taken by a committee of this House. The general manager of the Harris abattoir in Toronto, Mr. J. S. McLean-at that time the only concern manufacturing oleomargarine in Canada-referring to the ingredients entering into the manufacture of this article, said that it contained about fifty-five per cent of tallow, about 'fifteen per cent of creamery butter, fifteen per cent of cotton-seed oil, and a certain percentage of neutral lard, the exact figure he could not remember. *
A little further on he states that about 15 per cent of the finished product is the milk in which it is churned, because it is impossible to give it the proper flavour without churning it in milk. He also referred to the fact that they had purchased 3,659,000 pounds of creamery butter as a basis for this stuff in order to turn out this article of food. What was the price they paid for that butter ? The excuse was made that owing to the high price of butter it was necessary to introduce this stuff in order to overcome the difficulty. They paid for this quantity of butter, amounting to nearly 4,000,000 pounds, 37.36 cents per pound, for dairy, and 45 cents for creamery, that being the quantity of butter which they had in stock on March 31, 1919, when their financial year ended. He also made reference to the fact that they bought up a gieat deal of highly coloured June butter.
When he was asked why they bought butter at that particular season of the year, he said it was because they were not permitted to put any colouring matter into the margarine and that this' highly coloured butter gave colour to the article which they were putting on the market. He said:
The prices are so high, hut we have to buy a certain quantity in any event.
That is, the price of June butter was higher than that of butter bought at other seasons of the year, but he stated that they had to buy it in any event.
Of course we want that June butter for the oleomargarine, because it is a butter with a little colour and we need it for the oleomargarine, you know we are not allowed to put any colouring matter into the margarine and so we have" to use this June butter.
He was asked this question:
Why do you want to put it in?
That is the colouring matter. He replied:
We would like to, but we are not permitted to put in any colouring matter, so that we put in butter with as much colouring as possible.
This is a question I put to him:
You buy the June butter which is highly coloured to deceive the people. Is that not a fact? You realize that if it was sold without any colouring?

He said:
It would not be so palatable; it would be like eating lard.
This statement is made by the general manager of one of the largest manufacturers of this article in 'Canada. As he states, these people deliberately go out and buy highly coloured June butter in order to make this stuff look like butter. On previous occasions, I have stated that this was a deceptive counterfeit; that I had no objection to its being sold on its merits; nor do I object to its being sold on its merits; but if they want to smuggle it into the restaurants and hotels and have it consumed by the people of this country under the guise of butter, that is something that should not be countenanced by Parliament and the people of Canada.
This article was retailing at that time at from 40 to 41 cents per pound. How is it that the price of margarine at that time was almost as high as the price which they had paid for the butter which they mixed with it? Some time ago we turned loose on the people of Canada what is called a Board of Commerce, why have they not investigated the cost of and price of oleomargarine in this country. Why

has this board not investigated this matter in order to find out the cost of the different articles which go to make up this margarine as compared with the price at which it is being retailed to the public? It is true that one of the first acts committed by that board was to threaten the farmers of Ontario with dire consequences if they dared to increase the price of any of the dairy products. This was done in September of last year, at the end of the grazing season when it was well known that Ontario had the shortest grain crop the farmers of that province have had during their whole experience, when it was well known that the cost of production was going to increase enormously. I have proof of the truth of the words which I used on that occasion in the fact that grain for the production of milk has increased until oats have been selling at as high a price as $1.40 per bushel-I believe the market price is now $1.25,-that hay is selling at $40 per ton. Yet dairymen wefe threatened that unless they went on and sold milk, butter and cheese at the same prices at which they were selling those commodities during the summer months they would be fined and imprisoned.
Before I leave that question I should like to call the attention of the committee to some statements that were made at that time, that is, almost immediately after the appointment of the board. iSome hon. members may say that this matter has no direct bearing on the question before the committee; but my contention is that it has a direct bearing owing to the fact that protests are being made, not from one quarter alone, but from many quarters by those who are engaged in this business in which they have invested hundreds of millions of dollars. I quote from the Toronto Globe of September 14, 1919, an article in connection with an investigation that was being conducted in the city of Hamilton on that date by the Board of Commerce. Mr. O'Connor was credited with this statement:
This is not the time for an increase in prices. Prices should go down from now on. In this connection I wish to announce now that all vendors, from the farmer who increases prices on milk or anything- else, will be guilty of an indictable offence, punishable by a fine of $1,000 and two years' imprisonment.
We have heard about the cattle drives in Ireland. I will venture the statement that the Board of Commerce have driven more dairy cows to the shambles than were driven in Ireland during .the past fifty years. Is it any wonder that people would reduce their herds under conditions of that

kind with feed as scarce anid dear as it was and with the threat that they would be liable to suffer imprisonment for two years if they dared to increase the price? To find out what happened, all that it is necessary to do is to read the market reports for the next two months after that statement was issued. Tens of thousands of dairy cattle were driven to the slaughter houses and sold as "canniers" rather than that the farmers should carry on at a loss under conditions such as I have referred to.
There is another matter that has an important bearing on this question, and that is the production of bacon which is an adjunct of the dairy industry, at least, in the county from which ill come. As I stated at the outset, I do not know of a single factory in 6outh Oxford that is going to manufacture cheese this season, and I do not know of a single creamery in which a pound of butter will be produced, but I do know of manly farmers there who have not a hog on their farms to-day. That is the condition that confronts the people of this country when we are so greatly in need of greater production, and we may as well look the matter squarely in the face and not endeavour to evade the responsibility which must eventually rest upon us. I might quote here from an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Star of April 7.
One outcome of the active organized participation of farmers in public affairs is the growing rural conviction that " Labour " in the cities is slacking and soldiering at the farmers' expense.
The farmer has had the fact forced upon him that production in every line of activity Except agriculture has diminshed. Even with increased earnings industrial labour is producing less-and deliberately. The output of the average coal miner, for instance, has declined seventy-five tons per year. And so on down the line. The demand for shorter hours goes hand in hand with almost every demand for higher pay. Except for the farmer, upon whose production our life's necessities are based.
I do not think anyone will dispute the truthfulness of those statements. The demand for shorter hours certainly does go hand in hand with almost every demand for higher pay. We have heard a great deal about the necessity for building houses in the cities and towns, but our population has not increased so enormously as to cause any serious apprehension on that score, were it not for the fact that there are thousands of empty houses in the rural districts all over Canada. If you had those houses in the cities and towns, you would have no difficulty in housing all the people we have in this country. Let me read what

that great Canadian, the late (Mr. J. J. Hill, said a few years before he died:
When the people learn that all the wages In the world will not huy a pound of food unless somebody has gone out and by hard work raised that food, there will be more people raise food, and fewer people tell others how to do it. Hunger is our only remedy, and you will see it within twenty years.
The twenty years have not yet elapsed, but Mr. Hill was quite safe in saying that we should see hunger within that time. The war has no doubt aggravated the situation. I am satisfied that conditions at the present time are such as to demand sane action on the part of every one in this country, and frank statements as to what is passing in their minds, rather than an attempt to curry favour with some elements in the community. Hunger is our only remedy, says Mr. Hill, and you will see it within twenty years. To-morrow is the first day of May and seeding in Canada has scarcely begun. Weather conditions are such as to demonstrate that the farmer is possibly the greatest gambler we have im this country. The outlook is anything but promising, and I am satisfied, and I say it with all the force and emphasis at my command, the prospect is that hunger will be abroad in this country to a much greater extent inside of a year than it is at the present time. Unfortunately it will not be the rich who will suffer but the poor, jvho are likely to suffer for want of the very necessaries of life, and among these is butter for the growing children. I should like to see a movement on foot in this country to give the poor some special favours in regard to this necessary article of food, rather than a movement to wear overalls which will only result in increasing theh cost. It is quite common for some people in this country to take up some fad Which they think is going to be popular, and which will attract public attention to them. I was very much pleased to see the movement which has developed in this city and other places to boycott potatoes. Were it not for the fact that a boycott or something of that kind was in force at the present time I do not think there will be enough potatoes in this country for seed for this year. But I want to point this out. These people may defeat the end they have in view by adopting too much publicity in such methods. I notice by the papers yesterday that 34 carloads of potatoes were shipped to To-4 p.m. ronto, but in view of the agitation that has developed there, 28 of these carloads are being shipped to
the United States. That is the situation.
You will all remember how two years ago we were told in this House that if we adopted daylight saving, the people in the cities and towns would get out in the long evening and produce such a quantity of potatoes and other vegetables that there would be an abundance for everybody, and that the cost of living would be brought down to such an extent that daylight saving would be continued for all time to come. Some opposed the arguments that were advanced by these enthusiasts, who came mostly from the cities and towns. I believe that many farmers of this country took these statements seriously and relaxed their efforts in certain lines andi really believed that the cost of living was going to be reduced. I know that in 1918 quite a few enthusiastic people rented patches of ground and planted potatoes and other vegetables. They worked and sweated on the land, but in many cases they did not even raise as much as the seed they planted, and last year they devoted their time mostly to pleasure instead of carrying out the promises that they made to the people of this country. The situation with which we are faced is not confined to Canada. Unfortunately, it is world wide. It is the law of supply and demand that has created the demand for these products.
Last year we exported some 14,000.000 pounds of butter to other countries. Consequently, there was more than enough butter in Canada to supply the home demand. I have here a statement that was made by the Dairy Commissioner in Winnipeg a short time ago, as reported in one of the Winnipeg papers of February 20. He points out that the dairy industry of Canada amounted last year to $250,000,000, and that approximately $20,000,000 of that was for condensed milk, ice cream and powdered milk. You may pass regulations which will make it very difficult for people to carry on, but it is impossible to make them carry on if they make up their minds not to do so at a loss, and that is why it is foolish to attempt anything of this kind. In the constituency I represent they have not quit farming by any means, nor have they gone out of the dairying business. I believe there are more milch cows in the constituency of South Oxford than in any other in Canada. We have 48,000 of them in the county of Oxford, and almost the entire output of the county goes into condensed milk, milk powder, ice cream, and things of that sort, the value of which was $5,000,000 in 1919. You may put an embargo on

the exportation of milk from this country, and incidentally, there was an embargo ptaced on the exportation of dairy produce shortly after permission was granted to import and manufacture oleomargarine. I am sorry the hon. member (Mr. Crerar) is not in the House to answer for some of the things which he did when Minister of Agriculture. One of his first acts was to pas? legislation permitting the introduction and manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada. Shortly afterwards he introduced legislation to commandeer butter to send overseas. Did they commandeer the butter that was in cold storage, as was done in the United States where a similar measure had been adopted? Oh, no, that would never do. They commandeered the butter that was being manufactured from day to day, and they left alone the men who had purchased immense quantities and had big stocks on hand. A little later an embargo was placed on the exportation of milk from this coun-* try.
These are a few of the things I wiish to draw to the attention of 'the House as some of the difficulties those engaged in the dairying industry have to contend with. I am satisfied that when the statistics for the past year and for the present year are published you will find that there is going to be such a tremendous reduction in the dairy output of (this country that it will be startling to the peqple. You oannot expect those who are engaged in this industry to go on as they have been doing during the year® of the war. They have laboured for twelve, fourteen and sixteen hours a day in face of this fact we find embodied in the Peace Treaty an eighbhour day. Any one who knows anything about the dairy industry understands that it iis absolutely , impossible to conduct it under conditions of that kind.
In face of these facts we have the Minister of Agriculture coming 'before Parliament and asking us to approve of a resolution to extend for .another year the manufacture and importation of this article. I pointed out when ilt was first introduced *and when it (was to be for one year only that it would toe for iseveral years. The same was pointed out, last year bult they now say that conditions are no better today but worse than they were at that 'time.

My hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) has just charged me with want of courage, in being afraid to answer a question. I venture to think [DOT] that there are not many hon. members in this House who would back his charge. I leave him at that, and I do hope that he will subdue that objectionable one-tenith of his to which I referred the other day and allow the other nine-tenths to predominate for a moment.
I was saying when my hon. friend interrupted me that I am not at all sure that there is not as much dairying carried on in Red Deer as within those other two constituencies of South Oxford and Frontenac. If I took the sectional view I would go out to seek the support of the dairy men and women of Red Deer; but I am a free trader, and I take the national view, Mr. Chairman,. There is the difference. The national view is the good of the entire nation; it is the good of the consumer,-for we are all consumers. The sectional view is the good of the constituency which returns some hon. gentleman to Parliament; it is the good of some particular set of producers. So we find that both these hon. gentlemen (Mr. (Sutherland and Mr. Edwards) whom I have the honour to follow in this debate refer, quite naturally, not to the good of the entire people so much as to the good of the butter producers of their own districts. Well, all I have to say upon that point, Mr. 'Chairman, is that the glories of South Oxford, and of Frontenac, and even of Red Deer, mu^t be allowed to disappear when they stand in the way of the advance of human freedom and of the good of the entire nation of Canada.
Free trade asserts the right of every man and of every nation to buy in the cheapest and to sell in the dearest market, without the law interfering to benefit any given set of producers. But my hon. friends would make 8,000,000 people, who are all consumers, pay through the nose 75 cents a pound for butter and as much as could be wrung out of them by local producers of oleomargarine for the sake of a handful of dairymen in this constituency and in that. I do not suppose my hon. friend knew it, but it was. What is the ostensible object of the two hon. gentlemen? It is to defend some given industry. Well, Mr. Chairman, let me say that I am about sick of this talk of the ruin of our industries by the lowering of tariffs.
Hear, hear.

There never
was a better answer to an utterly false argument upon that subject than was supplied in the first instance by my hon. friend the minister (Mr. Tolmie), and was strengthened and emphasized by what fell from my hon. friend from Frontenac. At any rate, the one event has followed the other. Yet his whole purpose, as well as the whole purpose of my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) was to protect an industry which is supposed to be in danger. I leave their logic to them.
My hon. friend from Frontenac also pointed out that oleomargarine is selling in England or was selling in England at some period at 26 cents a pound while it was bringing 40 cents in Canada, and he seemed astounded at that. I cannot understand why he should have been. I have had the honour of being his colleague in this House for twelve years, and I have told him many times during those twelve years-I am afraid he is getting a little tired of hearing it theoretically-
Hear, hear.

-that the effect of lowering tariffs is to reduce prices. England is a free trade country. Why should my hon. friend be surprised if oleomargarine is only 26 cents a pound in England while we are paying 40 for it in Canada? Under normal, pre-war conditions that was true of everything.

Under normal conditions, under pre-war conditions, you could buy a scarf such as I am wearing and my hon. friend is wearing in England for 25 118
cents which you would have to pay nearly one dollar for in Canada. You could buy a suit of clothes such as he and I are wearing for three guineas, or $15, which you had to pay $30 for in Canada. So that my hon. friend really had no need to be surprised. But I want to thank him for his fact that oleomargarine was selling at 26 cents a pound in England when it was 40 cents in Canada. I want to point out, too, what a number of strange things we hear. When it suits the purpose of hon. members opposite, they tell us that the cost of living in England is as high as it is in Canada, but when some other purpose is to be served they tell us that oleomargarine is as twenty-six cents there to forty here. Now, Mr. Chairman, both these statements cannot be true. The fact is that the high cost of living in normal times is created in protectionist countries by the tariff. It presents no compensation in the way of higher wages or better conditions of living. It builds up the wealth of the rich; it increases the poverty of the poor. Jt lessens the means of support; it increases the price of everything the people buy which carries a tariff upon it. That doctrine il shall keep repeating and those who come after me will keep repeating until the flag of commercial as well as civil and religious freedom floats proudly over this fair and broad Dominion.
My hon. friend from South Oxford says that the time is particularly unpropitious for doing what the minister now proposes that we should do. Mr. Chairman, I take a diametrically opposite view. My hon. friend, in his Cassandra-like utterances, tells us that we are likely to have hard times in this country. I am very much afraid that that is true; I am very much afraid that in eighteen months or two years we shall have hard times in this country. If the history of the past is any guide to what is likely to happen in the future, then the destruction and the waste of war will be followed in this case ultimately by hardship and distress as they have always been in the history of the world. So I agree with my hon. friend as to the fact, hut I disagree with him one hundred per cent as to how we ought to face the fact-and I am glad that on this question at any rate the Government take my view. Why, Mr. Chairman, if we are going to have hard times, we have unrest now, and that unrest may pass to the verge of revolution. My hon. friend's suggestion is that to prevent that we should increase the price of the food of the poor.

I made no such
statement. I stated very distinctly-and the hon. gentleman must have heard me -that the only possible relief is to increase production.
Increase of production is another question altogether.

The effect of a tariff,
I have just proved, is to increase the price of the article carrying the tariff; my hon. friend must follow my argument. other farm products, and 'at the present time they have succeeded in raising the quality Of our butter to' a high standard.
