We are told to keep these female calves and raise them to cows, and now the Government says: We will let certain manufacturers make huge sums of money out of oleomargarine and compete with the farmers who have been trying to produce all the butter they could.
There is not a man in this House who has more sympathy for the poor than I have, but I want to say that it is due to the people in the cities and towns of this Dominion that food is dear, and that it will be dearer yet. Why are the boys leaving the farms? They are going to the towns and cities to work shorter hours. Who are responsible for these shorter hours? The people in the towns and cities are. Daylight saving has also something to do with it. Ask any young man in Ottawa or any other city whether he will work for five dollars on the farm or for five dollars a day in the city, and he won't look at the farm. He knows he will have to work twelve hours a day on the farm and only eight hours in the city. If I was a young man myself I would choose the city under those conditions. I hope I may toe wrong, but I believe the price of food will be doubled before a year or two, and then, because of the decreased production, there will be hardships in the cities and towns, and if it were not for the young and the old it would toe mighty little pity because they will toe themselves to blame. Sometimes a farmer after working fourteen hours a day and clearing 100 or 200 acres of land, feels when he reaches the age of fifty or sixty that life is getting short and that he -and his wife would like to spend the rest of their days in the city, and I have heard young men from twenty to twenty-five years of age say: They should not be allowed to come to the city; let them stay on the farm. Why, if the farmers of the Dominion of Canada had enough Gatling-guns to blow that kind of people into dust, it would be nothing more than people who would use such language deserve. Imagine saying such a thing to the men who have been

working fourteen hours a day helping to build up this country! I travel quite a bit, and the last couple of times I was home men have asiked me: "Where can I get a hired man; I have so many head of cattle and so many hogs. Try and get a man for me." One man told me that he got up at four o'clock last Monday morning, and after doing his chores went to the mill with a load of grain. It was only about ten o'clock when I saw him, and he had been back home and had another load. He told ' me that he had forty or fifty head of cattle, and he had his horses and hogs to feed. "I will have to do that at noon," he said. "But what shall I do about my seeding? If I cannot hire a man, I will just put in what I can, and if we produce only half the usual quantity we will get double the price." We are producing more cream than we get credit for, but where is it going? There is plenty of money in Canada. The Government is borrowing -money and using it in the cities and towns, -and 20 or 25 per cent of the cream that used to go into butter is now going into ice cream. Go into the ice cream parlours in Ottawa or any other city and what do you see? From seven to twelve o'clock at night you will see people who -complain that they are not getting enough pay, lined up for ice creams. They have lots of money to spend. I have heard the question asked,why is it necessary for the farmers to work twelve or fourteen hours a -day? People who ask that do not know what they are talking about. If you milk your cows at seven in the morning you have to milk them again at seven in the evening, because the cows should be milked at the same hour morning and evening. If cows were milked at seven in the morning and at five in the evening, every -cow in the Dominion would give at least one-sixth less milk, and butter and cheese. Who would be hurt then? Not the farmer, but the people in the cities and towns. You must milk cows at intervals of twelve hours to get the greatest flow of milk. I suppose some of these people think that the hired man should start work at seven and quit about five, and let the farmer and his wife milk the cows and feed the calves. But, thank -God, the farmers have got into a position where they can say, and they are saying it, and will continue to say it: We have this country by the throat; they had us by the throat long enough, but now we will defend ourselves. I think the Government ought to give very careful thought to the situation before proceeding with this legislation.

In some provinces, perhaps, there is not much dairying, but there is not a farmer in Dufferin county who is not a dairy man. No doubt they are small dairymen, but every farmer there has a dairy, and it is from a great many small farmers that we get the butter, not from one big producer. *Why my hon. friend (Mr. M. Clark) made the statement that there was more butter produced in the constituency of Red Deer-
In the province of Alberta.

-or the province of Alberta than in the province of Ontario, he surely must have known better. I have travelled through Alberta, and not one in a hundred farmers had a dairy. I had a relative out there one time, farming 600 or 5 p.m. 800 acres, and he kept only one cow. He told me he would not keep a cow any longer. He had 40 acres fenced in, on which he kept one horse and that cow, and he said that after he had done his day's work on his land he didn't want to stay and look after the cow, but wanted to be free to go where he wished. That is the kind of dairymen they have in the western provinces.

My hon. friend's hearing must be deficient or I must speak very indistinctly. What I said was that I should not be surprised if in the constituency of Red Deer there was a fair approach to the production of as much dairy produce as in the constituency either of Frontenae or South Oxford. I never said anything so absurb as that the constituency of Red Deer produced as much as the province of Ontario. It was only a tentative comparison I made between my constituency and the constituencies of my two hon. friends.

If I misunderstood the hon. gentleman, I accept his correction. I know that nearly every farmer in Ontario is more or less engaged in the dairy business. They are mixed farmers, and mixed farming is the best there is.
There is another reason why I cannot see my way clear to support this resolution. I am a moderate protectionist and always have been. All my life on the farm I have thought it was the only salvation for the farmer. I know that hon. members from Western Canada think differently, but I know very few men, whether they be Grit, Tory, U. F. O., or anything else, who will ,say in Ontario; We are free traders. Under free trade the farmer of Ontario last year would have lost on the average
$200 or $300 on hogs alone. That would pay all the duty on the clothes they wear for a good many years.
I notice that many men in the province of Ontario are. very careful about saying whether they are free traders or not. I am a moderate protectionist, a believer in tariff for revenue only, but I could not be consistent and say that with this 4 cents a pound on butter coming into Canada from the United States you should allow margarine to come in free also, in opposition to our dairymen. I am strictly opposed to it and I could not be consistent if I were not opposed to it. If the Government ever succeed in getting this resolution through the House, the only thing they can do, in order to be consistent, is to put a duty on the oleomargarine coming in. It would look mighty inconsistent if they did not do that.
I give this warning, that we are facing a serious situation as a result of the different causes that are operating to restrict production. The people living in towns and cities have no idea of the condition existing in the country. People, such as professional men, travelling through the country do not find it out; the farmers will not tell them, but when the farmers meet together and discuss the situation they realize that there is going to be trouble as a consequence of the fear that we are legislating to hold up the prices of oleomargarine as high as we can for the producer and pull it down as low as we can for the consumer. We must not do anything to discourage an industry upon which the life and soul of the nation depends. We were faced with a condition almost approaching starvation at some periods during the last four or five years. We were told that during the war and it is quite possible that with the mighty influx of population to the urban centres the time is not far off when conditions will be serious for the people of 'Canada.
Do not think that the farmers are worrying about the prices of farm produce'in so far as their food is concerned. They are making money on a good many things but they earn all they get. I will admit that some prices are high now but I tell you that it is the people in the towns and cities who will suffer if there is anything done that will stop production of farm produce. They will go hungry because the farmer will always raise enough for himself. I find that there is an agitation throughout Canada to keep these two elements in the community pulling apart. This agitation thrives upon the ignorance of the people of the cities and towns as to the conditions surrounding

production upon the farms. If we could get our people to pull more together, become more united and work more for the welfare of our country, it would be far better for us than having one class pulling one way and another class another way. There are too many men in Canada who are looking after their own individual interests. As long as a man can achieve his own ends that is about all he cares for. If any hon. member stands up and defends the agricultural cause he is defending the cause of more than half the people of Canada who are engaged in an occupation upon the success or failure of which the soul and life of the nation depend.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be
able to come to the relief of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) if my humble assistance can be of any help to him. It is unfortunate that the difference .of opinion on this question should take the turn of a difference between town and country. I think it is regrettable from every viewpoint and I am sorry that the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best) has endeavoured to draw the line, and make his fight, as between town and country. I sympathize to some extent with the view that he has expressed. The tendency of the times is too much to draw young men. away from the country and into the towns but I do not believe that the oleomargarine business has anything to do with it. My only complaint of the Bill of the minister is that it does not go far enough. He is temporising with the question whereas he should deal with it with a firm hand. I am reminded of the old saying:
Tenderly you grasp a nettle,
It will sting you for your pains.
Grasp it like a man of mettle Soft as silk it then remains.
My hon. friend has grasped the nettle gently; he is proposing to permit the use of oleomargarine for only one year more and that means that he will be bringing on a fight of this kind again next year providing this Government survives for another year. He is going to revive the fight, whereas I think we might as well have it out now and have it over. The dairymen have organized against this Bill. We have had evidence presented of their opposition to this measure and I am free to say that, while the views of our fellow citizens who are concerned with the dairy industry demand our respect and attention, they are not at all conclusive.

We are interested as the consumers. Everyone of us has to pay tribute to the dairy interest in the way of high prices for butter. If that tribute is a reasonable one we must not complain. We know that the dairymen represent an important industry; they are a large and intelligent body, they have invested their money, time, and labour in this industry and we are all concerned in seeing that they get a reward which will give them a decent and comfortable living and enable them to contribute to the prosperity of the country as a whole. We are all interested in maintaining the dairy industry of this country and if I believed that this Bill was going to hurt the dairy industry to serve some town interest I would cordially support the opposition to it. But I cannot see that the dairying industry is going to suffer in the slightest degree.
The dairymen in this matter are not wholly disinterested. They have their representatives in this House; their views have been presented to the House and we are bound to receive them with respect, But it is well that we should consider that in this matter they are not judges, but advocates of their own class, and we are not bound to receive their views without question. I do not really think that they have presented us with the correct view; I believe that they are mistaken. They will tell me that they know better than I do and I will not dispute that. But I am not able to see a single argument against allowing the people of Canada to use.oleomargarine if they want to use it, provided they buy it as oleomargarine and in accordance with such regulations as may be necessary for the purpose of guarding against imposition. There was reason, I suppose, many yeaa-s ago when a ban was imposed on oleomargarine.

Would the hon.
gentleman consider it an imposition to be permitted to mix from 15 to 35 per cent of butter with this commodity and to sell it as butter?

I would not like to
give my opinion upon that matter but I would simply say that I will support any reasonable regulation that can be devised to guard against substitution or unwholesome ingredients, and that will ensure a clean and wholesome product and ensure its being sold for oleomargarine and nothing else.

Then I am to assume that you are in favour of mixing but-

ter with oleomargarine in order to dispose of oleomargarine as butter?

No, that is a matter
of detail that I do not care to express an opinion upon. Any regulation that is made by the minister and that is designed to carry on this business under proper supervision, to guard against fraud and imposition, I shall support.

Would you have
these regulations made by Parliament, or by the minister, or by Governor in Council?
My hon. friend is generally more willing to have regulations made by the minister than I am. I am rather disposed to-

What about this
particular instance?

In this instance, although I have not the widest confidence in the present Government, still I am willing to trust them to make regulations of this kind-I am willing to go so far as that. I must say that if they are not fitted to make regulations concerning the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine I do not think they are fitted to govern this country.
Now at the time, many years ago, when this prohibition of oleomargarine was first imposed, it is but fair to assume there were good reasons for it. At that time oleomargarine was not as well known as it is today, and what was known about it was not too favourable, but I suppose there must have been good reasons-for the men who took that step were able men-why that ban was then imposed; but those conditions have changed, and for very many years I do not think there has been any good reason why oleomargarine should be shut out. So long as there was an ample supply of butter at a moderate price there was no reason, as a matter of common argument, why oleomargarine should not be shut out; so long as people could get butter at a fair price nobody bothered about oleomargarine or cared anything about it. But in the meantime, I think I am correct in stating, every civilized nation in the world admitted oleomargarine and Canada was the only country in all the world which banned it altogether.
I would remind the hon. gentleman that those, countries do not permit the mixing of butter with oleomargarine.

If my hon. friend is so set upon that question of mixing butter with oleomargarine I do not think I want to differ from him, but it is a matter of detail which can be dealt with in the regulations. The question is, shall we allow oleomargarine to come in like other products, or shall we shut it out altogether?
There is no country in the world which exercises more supervision over foodstuffs than Great Britain, and we know that oleomargarine has been an article of food there for many years. It is produced cheaply, comparatively speaking, in Great Britain, and before I conclude il shall perhaps give a reason bearing on that. What I want now to point out is, that while Canada has kept up this ban against oleomargarine the rest of the civilized world has abandoned it. Is it reasonable, therefore, to suppose that we alone are right and that the rest of the world is wrong? It reminds me of the old story of the man who sat on a jury and who said, "He had never met eleven such stupid men as those fellows" who differed from him. We in Canada, under the pretence of being better than the rest of the world at large, have been keeping up the ban on oleomargarine, when there has been no real justification for the course we have been pursuing.
It is not necessary to pretend that oleomargarine is as good as butter. Some hon. gentlemen opposite have declared that oleomargarine is not as good as butter. Nobody pretends or claims that oleomargarine is as good as butter, and so long as oleomargarine is sold for what it really is, nobody has any right to make such a claim.
I do not agree that the use of oleomargarine operates against the consumption of butter. My hon. friend from Dufferin has spoken very strongly from the farmers' point of view, and he has given us to understand that the use of oleomargarine is going to prevent the consumption of butter. I do not see it at all. Butter is selling-and it is selling to-day in Canada-as high as seventy-five cents a pound-we have been paying that in Ottawa very recently. The hon. gentleman tells us that it is selling at fifty or fifty-five cents a pound at some point in his constituency-it has been selling as high as seventy-five cents a pound in Ottawa. I do not say the farmer is getting too high a price, I do not say the farmer is a profiteer, I am not abusing the farmer in consequence, all I say is this: . that if I cannot afford to pay seventy-five cents for butter, and I am willing to buy

oleomargarine, why in the world shall I not ,be allowed to do so? That is the whole story.
It is not that I say that the farmer is getting too much; there is nothing to be gained in introducing that argument at all. But iif there are-and we know there are, although it may be chiefly in the cities and towns-thousands of families who will have to use oleomargarine or send their children to school without having partaken of anything approaching the character of butter at all, that is the whole story. It is not a conflict between oleomargarine and butter; there is no such conflict at all. There is an abundant demand for butter, and my hon. friend says there is an abundant supply. I hope he is right, but there is no doubt in the world that for every pound of butter that can be purchased in Canada to-day there is a ready market and a good price; nobody who can afford to buy butter is going to buy oleomargarine. Oleomargarine will only be used by those who cannot afford butter, and I do not 'believe that the consumption of it is going to reduce the production of butter on any farm in the whole Dominion of Canada.
There is one other point to which I wish to draw attention. I think the minister has made a mistake in not making this Bill permanent in its operation, and thus avoiding future trouble. As it is the minister is only nibbling at the matter now by granting this privilege for a single year.
My hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mir. dark) argued that the price was cheap in England because of free trade. I do not want to enter into a discussion of that phase oif the matter, but I desire to point out that the maintenance of the restrictions, referred to in this resolution, has a tendency to prevent people from getting cheap oleomargarine. The minister has told us that there are only two concerns in Canada that are manufacturing oleomargarine. The only wonder is that there are even two, because, under the prevailing restrictions, those firms have got to live from hand to mouth. If I were a manufacturer and desired to invest money in an oleomargarine factory what inducement is there for me to do so when this legislation is brought forward every year and has to fight for its life? Who is going to put money into any manufacturing industry which has no assurance of its existence? The very fact that there is po permanency, no fixity, attached to these conditions, that there is no fair chance for the oleomargarine manufacturer, that explains why oleomargarine is expensive. Remove these restrictions. Enforce all the

rules that are necessary for the sake of guaranteeing purity, but remove the restriction which threatens the manufacture and imporation of oleomargarine. Let any manufacturer in Canada feel that if he puts his money into an oleomargarine factory he has the same chance of success, so far as the Government is concerned, that he has in any other branch of industxy, and instead of only two concerns in this country we would have a dozen. And having a dozen concerns we might get cheaper oleomargarine, not as cheap perhaps as they have it in England, but certainly very much cheaper than it is now. I am delighted to be able in this instance to give my cordial support to the minister as far as he proposes to go; I only regret that he is not making this legislation permanent.

1
have the honour to represent a section of Canada in which exists I understand, the largest milk producers' association in the Dominion- I am not positive that that statement is correct, but I believe it is- an association whose membership consists of from one to two thousand milk producers. I have not received from that association any word of protest regarding the importation into Canada or the manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada. If they have lodged such a protest I know nothing of it. Even if that association should have presented any petition against this proposed legislation, I would feel it my duty to take issue with it at this time, but I do not believe they have done so.
With regard to the remarks made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland) respecting the value of milk, I presume every one fully endorses the position he takes. The association to which I refer is mainly a milk producers' association. True they produce a small quantity of butter and cheese, comparatively speaking, from time to time; but their chief object is to provide the largest possible quantity of milk for the coast cities. There are other milk producers than members of this association in the province of British Columbia, and no inconsiderable number of nonproducers are located in my own constituency.
When I think of the claims of both these elements representing two distinct sides of culture and life, I am compelled to support the Bill. I believe it to be right in principle. I believe that the people of this country should have the opportunity of purchasing such commodities as they desire when they are manufactured or im-

ported under proper Governmental supervision. As I see it the matter simply amounts to this: I am not able to buy a $100 suit of clothes; no man should say to me that I cannot buy a $40 or $50 suit. In other words, if I cannot purchase a limousine I should not be forbidden to purchase a common Ford. If men and women desire to purchase a commodity that may not be so good as butter, we must be very chary of saying to them: "You shall not do so."
Certainly, Sir, we believe in the rights of the individual along a great many lines. We say that within certain limits men and women should act as they see fit. And if there is one particular line in which they should have the right to act without undue interference, it is in the purchase of foods which are essential to the maintenance of life; and if they cannot buy butter, why should we say to them: "You shall not buy that which is second best"? In fact, Sir, I feel like endorsing the position taken by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). I am disposed to think that the country at large would support a measure which would say to the manufacturers of this commodity: "If you manufacture under conditions of Governmental supervision, go ahead and produce the best article you can, and put it, on the market in competition with the best product that our dairymen can produce." Let each compete and abide by the result.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. KENNEDY (Glengarry and Stormont):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution introduced by the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) involves a question of great importance to Canada, and should be taken into most serious consideration before being acted upon. The question involved is one of greater importance than we are likely to consider at first sight. It is not only a question affecting certain classes of producers and consumers; it is much more than that. It is not mainly a question of giving a certain measure of protection to the dairy industry by protecting his product in the home market on the one hand, or of affording to consumers an opportunity of procuring certain foods a little cheaper and thus helping them to solve the cost of living problem, on the other. It is infinitely more far-reaching than a question between the dairyman who produces butter and the labourer who wants oleo; it is a question that affects in its broadest aspects our whole national life, in that it strikes at the foundation of the growth, development and physical wellbeing of our people-the proper feeding of our growing population.
I would like to discuss this question in its broadest aspects and free it from the idea that it is a balancing of the best interests of the two classes to which I have already referred. Indeed, I shall immediately proceed to show that the prohibition of the importation, manufacture and sale of oleo in Canada does not afford protection to the dairyman in so far as the price received for his product is concerned; and that on the other hand to permit its importation, manufacture and sale does not, in any material degree, aid the poor consumer in solving the cost of living problem; and, furthermore, that its continued use by any considerable number of Canadians for any great length of time is fraught with hidden danger to the future physical vitality of our people.
The production of butter is doubtless one of the very important branches of Canada's agricultural activities at the present time. It is important from the point of view of the Canadian farmer because it affords him an opportunity of developing his business in such a way that the fertility of the soil is not depleted, thus leading to the establishment of a permanent system of agriculture in contrast to some other soilmining methods of farming. It is important from the point of view of the creamery-man and exporter because it affords them an opportunity for the profitable employment of their capital and labour. It is important from the standpoint of the Canadian consumer because it provides him one of the cheapest foods on the market at the present time, and at the same time one of the most essential nutrients for the growth and sustenance of the human body. It is important from the standpoint of Canadian finance because it is at the present time adding to the wealth of the country at the rate of approximately $50,000,000 annually and as a factor in keeping up a favourable balance of trade it is contributing its share by adding nearly seven million dollars to our exports. Indeed, it is unnecessary for me to recite further facts and figures in this connection because no one will question the great importance of the butter industry to this country.
It is well, however, to consider the one factor above all others which will determine whether this great industry will continue to grow and flourish and contribute to the prosperity of the country or whether it will decline, that factor is a profitable market price. In this connection it is well to know the influences that determine the

pound. If the nutrients in one pound of dozen eggs, or 2i pounds of beef or 1.73 pounds of smoked ham. So that if you pay 50 cents for a dozen eggs, you could buy the same amount of nutrients for the same money if butter were selling at $1.27 a pound. If the nutrient in one pound of beef are worth 35 cents, the nutrients in one pound of butter are worth 87 cents, and if the nutrients in one pound of smoked ham are worth 45 cents, the nutrient in one pound of butter are worth 78 cents, so that at present prices butter is much cheaper than most of the staple foods now on the market.
Another reason why it is dangerous to permit the sale of oleomargarine is because it leads to deception and fraud. Those interested in its sale have not shown a disposition to observe the law and regulations, but have persistently attempted to circumvent them, because there is such enormous profit in doing so. To substantiate this assertion I have only to direct your attention to the numerous convictions against parties for selling oleomargarine as butter instead of under its true character. In Hansard of Monday, April 26, you will find answers to some questions I asked in this regard, which shows conclusively that persistent efforts are being made to sell oleomargarine as butter and not as oleomargarine. Furthermore, the manufacturers of oleomargarine in their advertising propaganda persistently use the word butter, creamery, dairy, etc., in order to trade on the reputation of butter and mislead the consuming public into believing that they are receiving something just as good as the product of the dairy.
Again, the Dairy Industry Act of 1914 sets a certain standard for butter. It must be made of milk fat, salt and moisture and colouring substance, and nothing else can enter into its composition. Furthermore, from 80 to 84 per cent of it must be milk fat. It is illegal for a dairyman to buy cheap fats and mix them with butter and sell the product as butter. In this connection I am told that it is possible for the manufacturer of oleomargarine to buy large quantities of butter of the lower grades and mix them with other fats and sell his product as oleomargarine. This is surely unfair and an imposition directly on the dairymen. If it is just and fair that certain standards should be fixed to restrict the manufacturer of butter, and I agree it is, it is obviously unfair to expose him to the competition of another manufacturer

who can buy low grade butter and mix it with other fats and imitate butter in its texture and colour.
Now, iSir, I think I have said enough to establish the fact that in so far as the dairy industry is concerned we are not seeking any protection from any fair competition which we may have to meet. We do not claim that oleomargarine should be excluded in order that we should receive better prices for our butter; in fact, we know that its exclusion would not result in an increase in the price of our product. We do claim, however, that we as well as the consuming public should be protected from imposition and deception as now practised and permitted under the regulations. We would also direct attention to the fact that the alleged benefits to consumers are very small indeed, and that the whole question is fraught with very grave danger to the future health, growth and vitality of the Canadian people, and we therefore invite the fullest investigation and inquiry by the Department of Health into this phase of the question before any further action is taken in this matter.
At Six o'clock the House resumed and then took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock, and again went into committee on the proposed resolution of Hon. Mr. Tolmie to amend the Oleomargarine Act, 1919.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair

I shall not take up many minutes of the time of the committee on this subject but I should like to say a few words in support of the resolution which the Minister of Agriculture has brought in; and for fear that I may be said to represent a purely city constituency I would explain that perhaps one-third of my constituency is rural and in the farming sections of it there are two or three creameries. I wish to say that it is also a pleasure to support the hon. member for Red Deer who is, perhaps, one of the most important farming representatives in the House, and who is taking the same stand in support of the minister, while at the same time the member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) another representative farmer, is taking the opposite side. While agreeing with the former hon gentleman in his support of the minister I could not help but be struck, as we always are, with his eloquence, which we all appre-

eiate so much in this House, when the hon. gentleman approached the subject from the standpoint of free trade, as he always does, and proved that if we had free trade in Canada we probably would not need oleomargarine, because the price of butter would in all likelihood fall below that of oleomargarine. As the hon. member for Red Deer always argues so ably in support of his theory he finds in me, while listening to him, nearly always more or less of a convert; but I have got somewhat into the habit of checking up certain of the theories that he advocates, and upon going to the reading room just after the hon. gentleman began to speak, I obtained a Gopy of the London Times in order, if possible, to compare the price of butter in free trade England with the price of butter in protectionist 'Canada. After some search I found an item

the only one I could discover-in the issue of The Times of April 1 last, on page 21. This is the item referring to butter, which is contained in the market reports of the London Times of that date:
Butter-There is no change to report in either price or ration. Irish butter exporters have been recommended to charge 350s. per cwt. for choicest salted f.o.b. Ireland from April 1st, the price to be subject to revision by the trade each week.
Now, a hundredweight, Mr. Chairman, is, I understand, 112 lb., and dividing that into 350 shillings, makes the wholesale price- because the price I have quoted is the exporter's price in Ireland-exactly seventy-five cents a pound, and if we refer to the retail price in Canada-
What rate of exchange has the hon. gentleman adopted to make the price seventy-five cents?
I am speaking of the price in England.
You said the price in England was equal to seventy-five cents. What rate of exchange are you figuring on?
I am figuring on twenty-four cents to the shilling, which is the value given to it in England.
That is not fair.
The rate of exchange has nothing to do with it.
Sixty-two cents is right, not seventy-five cents.

I am figuring three shillings as equal to seventy-two cents, and there are three cents over, which would make seventy-five cents. The exchange has nothing whatever to do with it. Therefore the wholesale price of this butter in England- because the exporters are really wholesalers -is seventy-five cents. I was saying, when interrupted, that the price, so far as I know, in Ottawa at least, has never quite reached seventy-five cents retail. I thought it might be of interest to put that circumstance on Hansard.
I may say further-and I regret the hon. member for Red Deer is not in his seat, I should have preferred having him here to listen to my arguments-that in free trade England, not only the butter-makers but all other agriculturists have deteriorated in their business. In protectionist Canada the farmer claims1, and perhaps justly, that the duties on agricultural implements are a very heavy weight for him to carry around his neck, but it must not be forgotten that the wheat grower of Canada exports wheat five or six thousand miles to free trade England and undersells the grower of wheat in that country. Now, Mr. Chairman, I might finish that argument by saying the thought that strikes me is this: In view of the price of butter in England it might be a good idea from the Canadian dairyman's standpoint to get everybody in Canada to eat oleomargarine and export all our butter to free trade England and sell it there, because we can do so at an advance.
In regard to the importation of oleomargarine into Canada I think that now is the . time, if ever the occasion arose in this country, when we should find it very difficult to restrict the importation of this commodity for the reason that the prices of everything are so high. I understand that to-day the price of good oleomargarine is about 40 cents a pound as against butter at 65 cents a pound.
The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) who gave us a very interesting speech to-day, claimed that its importation caused hardship on the part of the farmers, and other speakers took the same stand. If I were at all convinced that the importation of margarine had really any effect of injuring our agricultural interests, I should without hesitation support any measure, which would prevent that injury; but when we consider that the price of butter to-day is 65 cents a pound, and before the war it was around 30 cents a pound-a little over one hundred per cent increase at least-and that all our butter supplies are finding a ready sale. I do not see that the farmer is suffering very much by reason of the use of margarine. And there is the advantage that the man

who does wish to use oleomargarine at a cheaper price has the privilege of so doing. In .fact, in private conversations carried on around the corridors of the House I have heard a number of hon. gentlemen make the statement that in their constituencies many of the farmers were using oleomargarine rather than butter.
Another point that struck me was the recollection that oleomargarine was the substitue for butter among our men at the front. My hon. friend from South Oxford said, as I recollect-he can correct me if I am wrong-that it was not those who were fed oleomargarine who went to the front and fought. I might turn that sentence around, Sir, and say:	That it was
those who went to the front and fought who used oleomargarine. I hesitate to use the trite saying, but one cannot help employing it:	That what was good enough
for the boys to eat at the front should at least not be unfit for consumption by those who remained at home. The hon. gentleman also implied it seems to me, by his words that the soldiers who did not use oleomargarine could have done better at the front than those who did. I think if the record of the Canadians is due to oleomargarine, it may be assumed that it would have been better for the Germans had they given more oleomargarine to their troops.
I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to put me in a wrong position. I stated that there was not a man who had gone overseas who had .been served with oleomargarine on his table at home.

I certainly do not wish
to put the hon. gentleman in a wrong position, but I think the first part of what I said was a fair interpretation of his statement; the latter part of course is more or less jocular.
The food value of oleomargarine has been discussed by several hon. members, and particularly by the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) who showed that the food value, according to the figures he had, was as high as the food value of butter, although he stated, I believe, that there were some vitamines in butter that are absent in oleomargarine. From the medical standpoint, I think that the small amount of butter which, after all, is consumed is not so important as a food as other fats which can be taken in its place. And the statement of one hon. gentleman that butter was necessary for growing children be-

cause of those vitamines or life-giving properties, is offset, it seems to me, by the fact that those qualities are amply supplied by the use of milk, even if children do not happen to get butter at certain times of the year, for most children in this country do get plenty of milk all the year round.
As to the taste, palatability and colour of oleomargarine, I cannot speak from having eaten it in this country, but certainly we ate large quantities of it in England and France, and many times we had disputes in England as to whether we were using oleomaigarine or butter. Indeed, 1 have seen people who claimed they were very good judges of butter unable to tell whether they were eating it or its substitute. At the same time I wish to support the hon. member for South Oxford and other hon. gentlemen wo endorsed him in his request that the regulations should be very strict to prevent the palming off of oleomargarine as butter. But I cannot see that the diluting of oleomargarine with butter should have any prejudicial effect so long as it is sold as margarine. The reverse of course should be illegal. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I have very great pleasure in supporting the resolution of the hon. Minister of Agriculture which has for its object extending the time for the importation and proper regulation of the sale and manufacture of oleomargarine.

The hon. member said also that in giving the figures respecting the increased production of butter in this country I had furnished an argument in favour of free trade. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) thought the Government was making a mistake in going no further, than extending the time for the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada; that the matter should be dealt with definitely and permanently. He told the Government that if they would only grasp the nettle firmly it would not sting them. Well, when the hon. member him-



self had the opportunity of grasping the nettle he took mighty good care that he did not touch it at all. During all the years that he had an opportunity of allowing the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine he took very good care to give the nettle a wide berth. The hon. member said that one reason why this should be made permanent was that the manufacturers of oleomargarine wanted to have an assurance that their business would be on a stable foundation. His words impressed me very much, and I took them down. He said: Who is going to put his money into manufacturing if there is no assurance of stability? That is an opinion which the hon. gentleman expressed once a year, I should say, during the fifteen years that he was Minister of Finance, and it indicates the policy to which he adhered pretty closely while he held that office. He has shown some disposition during the last few years to depart somewhat from that well-defined and very well-grounded principle. I agree that those who are engaged in any kind of manufacture should feel that their business will not be jeopardized by sudden changes; that it does not make for the stability of any manufacturing industry if there is uncertainty as to what position that industry will be in six months or a year hence. But if that is a sound economic principle,- and I believe it is-why should it not be applied to the dairy industry, which is one of the biggest industries in point of capital invested and number of people directly interested that we have in Canada? The dairymen have a right to ask the House to consider the enormous amount of capital which they have invested in the dairy industry, in the manufacture of cheese and butter, and they are entitled to an assurance of stability for their business and for the capital which they have invested. I know that the opinions of some other hon. gentlemen on this subject differ widely from mine, but with all due deference to their views I submit that the free importation of oleomargarine and its manufacture in this country does not make for the stability of the dairy industry, in which so much capital is invested and which has such a direct and important bearing on the industry of agriculture.

The discussion of this question, which has been under consideration by this House during the last three consecutive sessions, has given evidence of a decided variance of opinion depending on the interests involved respectively in what

we may call rual and urban municipalities. The (arguments of those who are interested in a cheap food for the labouring man have, from their viewpoint, some force, and the same may be said of the arguments used by those who represent the producers, unfortunate drifting apart of the people in urban and rural municipalities, of a lack of proper mutual understanding, not of their individual interests, but of what may be the great national interest. An industry which represents one-eighth of the total agricul-turarl production of the Dominion, namely, $250,000,000 out of $2,000,000,000, is an industry that is entitled to the very best consideration.
I thoroughly agree that it has been demonstrated already that the introduction of oleomargarine into this country under extraordinary conditions has not had that effect in reducing the price of butter that was anticipated at the time it was first introduced. But a force behind that, which is more injurious even than any forced reduction in the price of butter, is the unrest and uncertainty that prevails throughout the country districts by reason of the indefiniteness of the action or the intended ultimate action of the Government in regard to this matter. Last year when this question was before the House, I said that I hoped the Government would be able to see far enough ahead to know definitely whether this was going to be a final extension of the liberties allowed under this Act. At that time the Government gave the same assurance that the greatest safeguards would be thrown around the production of this substance and that precautions would be taken to guard against the possibility of its being used as a substitute for butter in hotels, restaurants, and so forth. Yet the minister (Mr. Tolmie), by his remarks in introducing the subject this session, would lead the House to believe that that colse study of the situation had not been given which would be necessary to enable the Government to determine even now what should be the ultimate policy in regard to this matter. The minister, speaking on Wednesday last, said:
Oleo is used to a very great extent by large numbers of poor people in the large cities and also in the country, and I consider that at the present time it is advisable to at least extend the Act for one year, and during that period to watch very carefully what measure might be adopted to put down the fraudulent use of oleo as butter. It is the intention of the department during that period to accumulate from other countries as much information as possible as to what is being done along this line, and to do their very best to apply this Act rigidly.

That is very commendable and desirable; but in my humble opinion-and we cannot blame the Minister of Agriculture for this- those efforts should have been put forth two years ago. The farmers of this country are very greatly disturbed on this question, possibly to an extent that is not justified. But notwithstanding that, the dairying interests are receiving a shock and are being retarded in their development by reason of these Acts of this House renewed from year to year, and the uncertainty as to what will be the ultimate decision. That is the greatest misfortune and the greatest objection to this Bill. If it were in the power of the minister to say to-day: We are going to extend this for two years, and if he could give the dairying interests an assurance of what would happen at the end of that time, I would be willing to support the measure rather than support a measure extending it for a year, as is proposed by this Bill, and be left in uncertainty as to what is going to happen at the end of that period.
The people of the rural districts and of the cities must endeavour to understand each other better. The people of the cities must not live selfishly to themselves; neither must the farmers. Because the interests of both are after all mutual in the great national upbuilding of this country. I fancy, if they could get together on this subject, and if it could be shown that the agitation and annoyance caused to the agricultural community by these Acts had a deterrent effect on the development of the industry, the city people would realize that the introduction of this oleomargarine was to their ultimate disadvantage. The cost of the quantity of butter any labouring man consumes is a matter of infinitesimal consequence in comparison with the much larger wages he is drawing to-day than he was in years gone; and if labouring men in the cities knew of conditions in the country and how seriously this affected the dairying interests, they might be more willing to forego to some extent their selfish interests and understand that it was in the national interest to increase the production of the real commodity rather than to have this spurious article put on the market to help them out.

not ask that any guarantee be given to the manufacturers of oleomargarine with regard to the tariff. May I call my hon. friend's attention to one point?
Yes.

I think my hon. friend has overlooked one thing. He said that when he as in office there was not any need of people looking for oleomargarine because the price of butter was not high. The hon. gentleman has forgotten that very full report which was made by his present leader (Mr. Mackenzie King)-then Minister of Labour in the Laurier Government -which stated that the prices of foodstuffs were so high at that time that the people were on the verge of a revolution. I am sure he will admit that that report influenced him to open the doors and let butter, and all other kinds of foodstuffs come in free. Such was the situation then. It is true that during that time-taking a period of twenty years-the price of dairy butter had run from as low as ten cents a pound to as high as twenty-two cents a pound, an average of sixteen and a half cents a pound; and the price of creamery butter ran from sixteen to thirty-two cents a pound, or an average of twenty-two cents a pound. Notwithstanding that, the then Minister of Labour-now the present leader of the Opposition-said in the report referred to that the prices of foodstuffs, including butter at an average price of twenty-two cents a pound-were .so high that the people of the country were on the verge of revolution.

My hon. friend is getting away from the point. My statement was that during the whole fifteen years to which the hon. gentleman referred there was no question of removing the ban from oleomargarine. I sat in the House with my hon. friend, and you may depend upon it if there was any public opinion clamouring for the removal of the ban at that time my hon. friend himself, I am quite sure, would have heard of it. At all events, during our period of office, there was a strong party in the House differing from us. And I repeat the statement now, that during the whole fifteen years-to the best of my knowledge and belief-no request was ever made to the Government to remove the ban from oleomargarine.

We have heard a good
deal of discussion in this House, not only during the present session, but last year, and doubtless on other occasions, and a great many hon. gentlemen have taken part in that discussion. Many of them have expressed the desire that the people should be free to use oleomargarine as an article of food, but I believe it is only proposed to extend the privilege of importation and manufacture for another year. After that, as I understand it, this will be no longer permitted. If moTe than that were proposed I would certainly feel it my duty to offer this legislation very strong opposition, because from all that I can see its effect would be nothing less than the destruction of the dairy industry throughout Canada. In the part of Canada from which I come the farmers have to use their utmost knowledge and ability to achieve success in carrying on the industry of agriculture. It is imperatively necessary for them in doing so to raise live stock and thus provide fertilizer for the land. If the dairy industry were wrecked it would undoubtedly kill the great farming industry of the country. The concession which is now proposed may help labourers in the city to a' certain extent. When butter was sold at twenty-five cents a pound those labourers were in receipt of a daily wage of $1.25 to $1.50; but it must be remembered that, even though the price of butter has now mounted to fifty or sixty cents a pound, the wages of those labourers have been augumented to $3 or $4 per diem. There is a great,deal of talk about the price of butter, but why is there no outcry about the price of sugar, or the price of meat? Meat is a necessary food for men engaged in strenuous labour, and yet it is
twice, or three Or four times, what it was in years gone by. The enhanced price of meat and other foodstuffs has contributed to the high cost of living. But I do not think the remedy for that is to cut down the dairy industry and to handicap the farmer in the operations he carries on.
In our part of the country the dairy industry is a most important one, perhaps the most important in connection with farming, and having the preservation of that industry in view I say it would be the part of prudence not to open the doors to the importation and manufacture of this inferior food. Even though it might be five or ten cents a pound cheaper than butter it cannot possibly take the place of the latter as a good and wholesome article of diet.

Notwithstanding the reference which has been made by my genial and much respected friend from Carleton county (Mr. Boyce) as to the lawyers taking part in this discussion yet, as a member of that despised class I want to say a word or two on behalf of the consumers who live in the large cities. The discussion so far has gone rather far afield.
I support the resolution for these reasons:
If the resolution were defeated it would mean the total exclusion of this commodity, and it seems to me that such a result would be directly against the interests of our people. I say that because, although it has not come out in the course of the debate, the original statute passed in 1914 provided that:
No person shall manufacture, import into Canada, or offer for sale, or have in his possession any olemargarine.
If we defeat the resolution that is the condition of affairs that we must go back to. I am quite certain that in large centres where people have learned the value of this article as a food they would deeply resent any action which tended toward the total exclusion of oleomargarine.
In 1914 when this legislation was passed the dairymen were apparently on top, and . they were able to secure the adoption of their views because at that time a prejudice existed against oleomargarine. But we have been told by an hon. member who served at the front, that oleomargarine was the only food of this kind that the soldiers had at the front, and they liked it as well as the butter they had been used to in Canada. Another hon. member stated today that he had tasted oleomargarine in a high-class restaurant and thought he was eating butter.

I shall not attempt to go into the question of the relative nutrients and calories contained in oleomargarine and in butter; I leave that question to be dealt with by those who are conversant with food values. It is sufficient that our people believe that oleomargarine is a good food, and I know that thousands of people in my constituency desire the privilege of purchasing oleomargarine simply because they cannot afford to pay the higher price for butter, and they are quite satisfied with this substitute.
I am also confirmed in my view by the opinion of women, who, we must admit, are the best judges on these domestic questions. We have been told that a circular was put on our desks a few days ago by the National Council of Women, and it has been condemned as an improper proceeding. Well, I think it might be very well excused, as the ladies are not yet versed in the rules of this House, and I am quite sure that this propaganda work was done quite innocently and not with the idea of offering any affront to our traditions. As I say, it must be conceded that women are supreme in the domestic realm, and the National Council of Women is a body of experts on domestic questions. They make a study of these problems, and it is seldom that anything printed in their magazine or spoken at their meetings is open to criticism. Therefore it is higly important, to me at any rate, what position those women take upon such a question as this. They have compared oleomargarine with butter, they have studied the needs of the poorer classes, and they are strongly in favour of not excluding this article of food from the homes of the poorer people. These women experts are unselfish in their study of economic questions such as this, and as they having definitely come to the conclusion that our people need this article, I would be very reluctant to oppose them in the stand they have taken.

crease in our butter production ft does not .look as if our dairy interests were hurt by allowing our poor people to buy oleomargarine.

speechtext:
Yes; 194,904,336 pounds. 1 would like to ask my hon. friend, how much we have increased our manufacture of condensed milk? Dairy products do not go into butter and cheese only.
* Mr. SEXlSMTTH:	I am not opposed to
the poor man getting margarine, but I am opposed, as the hon. member for South .Oxford says, to the mixing of butter in oleomargarine and selling dt to the public-I do not care under what name.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to this discussion, and when I remembered the speech delivered a day or two ago before the Agricultural Committee by Dr. Robertson, wheb he stated the seriousness of the food situation of the world, [DOT]I felt that I could not oppose the poor man having oleomargarine. Therefore, when the painister announced that he had decided to extend the time for the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine another year I did not care to interfere. But I want to [DOT]say to hon. gentlemen to-night that the poor people we have heard so much about to-day are buying butter fat in the city of Ottawa every day by the thousands at the rate of $5 a pound, and not saying a word about it-in the ice-cream parlours. That ds all right; I am not complaining about it. But when we hear so much talk about the price oif butter, I want .to say that the farmer in Ontario producing butter to-day, and butter only, does not make 50 cents a day for a 12-hour day selling his product at 60 cents a pound,-and the hon. Minister of Agriculture knows it.
I think we should go very carefully when we are dealing with matters of this kind to be certain that we do not discourage our farmers, for there never was a time when we wanted greater production and more production than to-day, if we are to save Canada and the Empire. According to Dr. Robertson we are practically facing world starvation, and if Providence is not good

to us this year in granting an abundant harvest on this continent, millions of people will be facing starvation.
I do not care to go into derails, hut really the letters we 'get in connection with oleomargarine would make any honest, sensible man laugh. I received the other day a long communication, covering two or three foolscap pages, from the Retail Merchants' Association, and, would you believe it, Mr. Chairman, they say that the manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada has already raised the price of hogs one dollar per head and price of beef and cattle two to three dollars per head. Well, that is all in the interests of the farmer, but what an argument to advance.
Now, I have no objection to people using oleomargarine that is oleomargarine and not butter. If they care to eat that product, surely they should have it; I sympathize with them for having to eat it. I read in a magazine some time ago that in 1917 some 20,000,000 pounds of whale oil were used in Sweden in the manufacture of oleomargarine. Whale oil may make good oleomargarine; the food thus produced may be quite wholesome. A friend of mine was telling me a week or ten days ago* that he had read an article in some paper which stated that the fat taken off beef hides was being used in the manufacture of oleomargarine. A few days afterwards he happened -to be in a tannery while they >vere removing the oil off the top of the fat. The men in the tannery pointed out that nothing of that kind was now wasted. He said that he immediately thought of the article he had read a day or two before, and thought: If that is what is going into oleomargarine, no oleomargarine for me. However, if the minister surrounds the manufacture of oleomargarine with strong safeguards and prevents the mixinig of butter with it, I will support the resolution for this year.
The hon. member says that oleomargarine is sometimes made from the fat which is scraped from hides.
Well, I did not say that was done; I was giving somebody else's statement.

So far as Canada is concerned, this is impossible. All oleomargarine manufactured in this country is made under the closest supervision of our Meat Inspection Branch, and only fats of first-class quality are included. With regard to oleomargarine ruining the dairy industry, I may say that its manufacture did not
have that effect before, during, or after the war in many countries where oleomargarine has been manufactured for a number of years. In fact, in one of the .best-known .butter countries in Europe, Denmark, oleomargarine has been manufactured and used ,for very many years. The farmers there export their high-class butter to the London market and use oleomargarine. Another striking fact is that while oleomargarine has been manufactured and sold in this country for the last two or three years, cattle are still very high in price, and the same is true of butter. So far as the regulations are concerned, the Department of Agriculture proposes to prevent fraud as far as it is possible to do so. Judging from the arguments that have been advanced on both sides, the greatest objection to oleomargarine lies in the fact that it is very often sold .as butter. To overcome that we are insisting on having the word "oleo" stamped clearly on every package, into the very article itself, so that the name cannot be removed with the wrapper. Moreover, we have increased the minimum fine for any offence against the regulations from $10 to $50. In addition to that, arrangements are under way which are designed to make the inspection very much closer than it has ever been.

Is it the intention to permit the packing of oleomargarine in identically the same packages as butter? And are the manufacturers of oleomargarine still to have the monopoly of the right to mix butter with another product?

I have received a suggestion from a certain dairy organization asking that the size of the packages be increased; that matter is under consideration. We have not permitted the manufacture of oleomargarine in butter factories for the reason that it is most difficult to keep track of such factories. The abattoirs in which oleo is made are undeT the constant supervision of the Meat Inspection Branch.

Judging from the number o.f speeches made on both sides of the House and the variety of opinions expressed, I am disposed to think that there will be a division on this resolution, and I do not care to give a silent vote.
The difference between oleomargarine and butter is a difference which exists in connection with many other articles that enter into the economy of life. If a man cannot buy butter and is obliged to buy the next best thing that he can get I do not think that

we should put any obstacles in his way. If he and the members of his family like oleomargarine, and that product is found to be healthful and nutritious food, I do not see why he should be prevented from buying it. The same thing applies to many other phases of life. When travelling on a railway train some people use the second-class coach, some the first-class, some the parlour car, some the drawing rooms. I suppose they would all like to travel in the drawing rooms and parlour cars, but if they cannot afford to do that they do the next best thing; they cut their coat according to their cloth. Surely we should not say to the man who is travelling in a second-class car: You have no business to travel here; you must go into the more expensive cajs; the Government want to make more revenue out of these railroads; consequently, you may not travel as you like; you must travel as we order you to. travel. Many of us would like to wear 'broadcloth, to dress in purple and fine linen, hut we may be able to afford nothing better than homespun and overalls. We would like the higher class of goods, but if we cannot afford them it is nobody's business to interfere with our making the most of our income. If the farmers expect a monopoly of the market for butter and dairy products, . they must rise to the occasion and supply those products at reasonable prices. That applies not only to butter, but to all articles of production or manufacture.
I was rather pained to hear some hon. members object to a little butter going into this oleomargarine. I thing if is cruel to say that the poor man (who cannot afford to buy the good butter should not be permitted to give any butter at all to the little family sitting round his table. If a little butter goes into this product, surely it is better for those who consume it because that butter is in it, and it is to that extent a market for the people who produce butter, So that they axe not suffering in that regard. Good butter need not, of course, be afraid of competition in the open market with oleomargarine, and therefore there .should be no objection to making this article as good as possible if we are going to have it at all.
This question opens up, to some extent, the question of the high cost of living and involves questions of domestic science and relations, etcetera, which have been discussed on this occasion. I would draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the wider scope of the subject with which we are dealing. We are complaining and,

I think, properly, of the high cost of living generally and the very high prices of articles that men who live and have families must have. It is extraordinary that those prices are soaring so high and yet nothing is being done in an endeavour to curb them. For some years, we have been discussing in this House a court that would have some control over those prices. We got that court, and I am sorry to say that it does not seem to be receiving the support that the Government should give it. The chairman of that court has resigned; the court has been broken up and to some extent demoralized. The law which it has been administering has been found fault with by the Supreme Court, and its decisions have been rendered ineffective by reason of some defect in the statute. My experience of courts and laws is that if a high court finds that a statute of any Parliament does not furnish the machinery that was intended to be furnished and that it is weak or defective, Parliament at once comes to the rescue and furnishes the material necessary to' perfect that statute so far as its weakness has been revealed by the decision of the court. If a recent decision of the Supreme Court has shown weakness in the Act constituting the Board of Commerce, it is our duty at once to come to the rescue and complete the machinery that is proposed to afford relief to the people bf this country who complain of high prices. This is exactly along the line we are discussing in regard to food products, of high prices and what shall be done to make the cost of living lower so as to show that we have an interest 'n these things, and that, Imerely because we may ourselves individually get along without very much trouble iwe are not forgetting our brethren who .may not be equally favoured. The prices of sugar, potatoes, flour and so fourth are simple matters with which we could deal .and with Which the Board of Commerce could deal if it were property equipped for that work, if it is not so now. We 'should keep that court fully manned, and if there is any weakness in the Act, that weakness should be removed. It is only within a very few days that I received communications from certain parts of the country to the effect that potatoes which were selling for $1 a bushel all summer, all at once went to $3.50 per bushel,

speechtext: I must call the hon. member to ordeT and remind him that we are at .present discussing the resolution before the committee.

I stated that I thought this question Opened up for discussion these other questions, and I think it would be at the stage when I made that statement that I should be called to order. I do. not wish to be out of order; but if we are discussing foodstuffs, and if we are manufacturing oleomargarine because it is necessary in order to help the poor people aJlong, I should think I was in order in bringing those matters to the attention of the Government. The minister, of course, finds me all wrong, but I am coming nearer the holy circle of the Treasury benches. I know that, although quite out of order, I have said enough to convey to 'the leader of the House (Sir George Foster) my opinion, and even though it is conveyed in that disordered manner, I hope he will take notice of wha't I have said.
As regards this resolution, I have only to say that, while there are thousands of farmers in my riding and I have to account to those farmers for anything I may say or do in this House, I say to my farmer constituents that, if they are not able to produce enough butter to furnish the people of this country with that very excellent article at a price within their reach they must not find fault with the Government for (permitting some other article to be manufactured and produced in Canada which the labouring (people and others who are not themselves producing can buy at a price that is not beyond their reach. My good friend from New Brunswick (Mr. Leger) said a moment ago that a difference of fifteen cents per pound was not worth speaking about. In a large family, about two pounds of butter per day is required; that is not big consumption, and that means thirty cents a day at even fifteen cents, and in a run of seven days that would amount to $2.10. Now, $2.10 out of the poor man's wages at the end of the week is a considerable amount, and if the difference is only fifteen cents per pound, if oleomargarine answers the same purpose for him and his family as the higher priced article, if it comes to the point where I have to vote on this question, I will support the resolution of the Minister of Agriculture.

'Sir GEORGE FOSTER:	The explanation of that item is this: there is a capital account in conection with the elevators. This item is not for maintenance, for the replacing, for instance, of machinery that is worn out; all that comes from the revenue itself. But if one of the elevators is not equipped with drying machinery, for instance, that is charged

At what points are

Vancouver,
Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, and the elevators at the head of the lakes.
All in the West.
Yes, those that are under my department. The Railways have an elevator at Port Colborne, and there is a small one at Halifax. There was one in St. John, but it was burnt down.

There are questions
concerned with the Halifax elevator, but I presume they should come up on the Estimates of the Department of Railways.
Does the minister collect fees from these elevators?

Yes. I think
it might be interesting to the House to know that for this whole service our permanent staff is 224, and the temporary staff 255, or 479 employees altogether. The pay for this staff amounts to $652,096. The expenses on the whole grain operations, including elevators, for the past fiscal year amounted to $937,521, and the revenue was $1,082,062. Taking all the elevators and their operation the whole grain staff employed in inspection, weighing, grading and everything connected with the operation of the elevators is paid for by the fees from these two branches, inspection and weighing fees, and the like of that, and there is a fairly good balance on the right side.
Why does the minister want more money if he has a balance to the good?

When we get a vote we spend the money that Parliament gives us. The revenues are not spent as they come in by the department. Everything that comes in has to go into the consolidated revenue fund account. We cannot take out of that. We spend out of the vote that Parliament gives us and we put into the consolidated revenue fund everything that comes in. We do not handle any of the money at all; that goes to the bank.
It is not like the railways.
This has a balance on the right side.

The expenditures were $937,000 and the revenue $1,082,000 in round figures.
When will the minister fix the locus of the court of appeal in wheat grading and will he say whether it is to be at Port Arthur or Winnipeg?

Although the
legislation has passed constituting a court of appeal it has not as yet been put into effect. It goes into effect upon a proclama-

tion being issued by the Governor in Council. Appeals from the decisions of the inspectors in respect to any grievances are dealt with by the old board of survey which has been in existence for a number of years and which has done that kind of work up to the present time.
Is it the intention of the minister to take advantage of the legislation and establish this court which was thought necessary when the legislation was passed?

It was a matter of legislation and was considered therefore a fit subject to be carried out practically. But it is a board which will bring a good deal more of expense and that expense is to be borne by the grain producers themselves. The comparatively small number of cases which come before the survey board, the very good manner in which they have carried on their business of examination and given their judgment in these matters, rather incline the Government not to incur the expense at present. Whilst there are two opinions about it in the West there has not been a very strong pressure to have a court of appeal established.

I noticed that when the Bill went through the House there was a vigorous competition between the head of the Lakes and Winnipeg. At the next session I was bold enough to say to the minister that he found it embarrassing to decide between these two factions and consequently the Bill was not brought into play. Possibly that has something to do with the economical ideas of the minister.

If my hon.
friend's memory is as good in all respects as it is in that one he will recall that I very decidedly repudiated that as the motive in the matter. I am ready to give a decision whenever it is thought advisable to have the court constituted and brought into operation.
The advisability and the establishing of the court are both in the power of the minister, and who shall come to tell him about the advisability? It rests with him entirely.

Parliament gave that discretion to him and he will try to exercise it in the best possible manner.
Canada Year Book, 113,500.
Is this money expended for staff, or printing, or to collect information?

The information is collected by the staff of the Bureau of Statistics and the cost of the Year Book is the cost of the printing. There is nothing paid for the matter which goes into it. We get some very valuable monograms which are contributed by the writers without pay. Nothing is paid for the matter in the book. Yes, I think that is so. If it is not so I will make a note of it and let my hon. friend know.
Is there any revenue from the book?

There is not much , revenue. It is distributed quite largely to members of Parliament, libraries and boards of trade. Although there is a nominal price placed upon it the revenue which comes in from that source is not very large as is the case with most of our publications. We are striving now with several of the departments to limit the number for free distribution and increase the number that may be purchased by the public. There is a gradual increase in that respect although it is not very large. I think we ought to strive to make it much larger. With a book of that kind we are subject to quite a number of exchanges because we get similar books from different bodies and we must reciprocate. We make a pretty free distribution amongst libraries, chambers of commerce and institutions of that kind.
In Canada?
In Canada and outside of Canada.
No copies are sent abroad?

Yes, we send quite a large number of copies abroad, to the British Dominions and to a number of the principal countries as well.
