Development and Extension of Canadian Trade, $130,MO.

This is a very important vote, but J notice it has been reduced by $20,000. Unless there is very good reason why this amount should be reduced from $150,000 to $130,000 it seems to me this is not very good policy on the part of the Government. If there is anything we all desire it is to see our foreign trade extended, and I would therefore like the minister .to explain why this vote has been reduced.

The vote asked this year is for $130,000, a reduction of $20,000 from the vote of last year. The expenditure up to the 29th February, 1920, is $74,541. The details of the expenditure for 1919-20 include these items:	Industrial
moving pictures, including the purchase of films, cameras, chemicals and photo supplies generally; also salaries and travelling expenses of officials, $42,911; exhibition of industrial moving pictures in Canada, $4,623. An exhibition of Indian hides accounted for a small amount; and the Lyons fair and the Paris exhibit took $24,794. In addition there were the expenses on a mission to Spain of one of our commissioners,

Mr. Clarke. These items make up the amount of $74,541, that was provided for the extension and development of Canadian trade, and was expended last year along those lines, although it does not cover the amount expended for the whole of the services of the Canadian Trade Commissioners -we will come to that a little bit later, and my hon. friend will find there is a very considerable vote for the purpose. I am quite in sympathy with the idea that this is one vote as to which, at this particular time, we cannot afford to be too economical, and we have made what is considered a very generous estimate for that work. We must take into account the fact that during the last four or five years-four years anyway-the services of the trade commissioners have been to a certain extent interfered with, and on account of the war, we have been out of a number of countries where we had missions before. Now that the war has ceased and conditions are coming towards normal we are occupying again most of those countries, and we are also getting into other countries as well. Probably it might be just as Well for me for a few minutes to give an idea of the scope of our work to the extent that it has been undertaken for the present time. Outside of Canada, where we have our central offices and from which we direct our work, our trade commissioners in Great Britain are located in Glasgow, London, Bristol, Birmingham, Liverpool and Manchester. These trade commissioners have been carrying on their work there for a number of years, and they are now particularly active under the new conditions which are arising, resulting in part from the war. We have made an extension in Paris, with the idea of covering France. We have added to the High Commissioner's office there a trade commissioner who will devote himself particularly to the extension of 'our trade in France, and will give the whole of his time to trade work.
We have taken up our position again in Belgium and in Holland, where for the war years an office was simply kept but no particular trade work was possible to be done. We have a trade commissioner at Milan in Italy, one of our most capable young men, and we are using him at the present time in making a survey of conditions as they are along the Mediterranean coast. He extended his work so as to cover Spain for two or three months, and has made a very thorough study of conditions there-as thorough as it could be during

the time he devoted to it. His report, which is a very valuable one, is being published and given to our business men. At the present time, besides carrying on work in Italy, we have had him for a month in Greece looking into the conditions there- coming into contact with the business men, and making for us an investigation out of which will come a report as to trade possibilities in Greece.
Mr. Wilgress, who was in Vladivostok, has been recalled from there and with Mr. McLeod Clark is now making a pretty thorough examination of the conditions for trade possibilities and preparing for us the information which they got in the shape of reports from the countries along the Mediterranean border, and in Southern Russia, and in the new republics of Serbia, Czecho-Slovakia and Poland. These two men will be engaged for the next five months probably in making a very thorough survey of conditions in those countries where there are large possibilities opening up for our trade. The countries bordering on the Mediterranean we had very little to do with before the war, hut during the war we conducted extensive and very profitable operations with Rou-mania, Greece and Italy. The trade possibilities in that section of Europe are large and in future will. I think, tend a great deal to the advantage of our exchanges.
Then we have in Australia one of our oldest and best trade commissioners in the person of Mr. Ross, at Melbourne, and he has an assistant at Sydney. We have a trade commissioner in New Zealand, Mr. Beddoe, who was appointed sometime ago and who is doing very excellent work there. We have in China, a trade commissioner with a central office at Shanghai. In Japan we have one of our young men who was first trained in our university here, in our own department afterwards, and who is now engaged in his work in that country.
I may say that I am making it a sine qua non that the men who go to these foreign countries shall become thoroughly acquainted with the native languages. Our trade commissioner in Italy has now a comparatively thorough knowledge of Italian, he is also proficient in French, and for the last two or three months he has been studying Greek and is able to talk in a colloquial sense in that language. In the same way our agent in Japan, who was born in that country as it happens, is making himself thoroughly acquainted with the language. We have a commissioner in Brazil, a late appointment, and he has already made himself familiar with the language which is spoken there. Then we have a commissioner in Buenos Aires, a Mr. Webb. These gentlemen,, together with the commissioner in the West India Islands, with a central office at Barbadoes, and a commissioner lately sent to Cuba, make about the tally of trade commissioners in the foreign field.

It struck me that the commissioners mentioned are at very distant points, in the Far East, in Australia and in the Argentine, whereas we have nq commissioners in the neighbouring republic. Would my hon. friend favour placing some commissioners in the United States to promote trade with that country, which trade is so much larger than can possibly be developed at those distant points. Why should we go to the ends of the earth looking for trade when it is at our doors? For example, we purchase about $2,000,000 worth of goods a day from the United States and sell them roughly * about $1,000,000 worth a day. Does not the hon. minister think that the appointment of trade commissioners in the big trading centres, such as Chicago, New York and Boston, would enable us to widen our markets in that country and even restore the balance of trade in our favour? It is the greatest opportunity that we have, and in looking over this long list it strikes me as rather extraordinary that we do not find any trade commissioners in the cities of the United States. I think there is a representative of some kind in Washington, but in the interests of our trade with the United States would it not be well to have commissioners stationed there to help us develop our sales to that country?

My hon. friend has raised a question which has often been before the department. Where you are so close that you can speak to your neighbour from your own doorstep it is not necessary to have an expensive organization. I have always taken the ground that the facilities for intercourse, and the information and knowledge so easily passing backwards and forwards between Canada and the United States, render it unnecessary for us to incur a heavy expense in establishing trade commissionerships in that country. The trade between ourselves and the United States is a trade between two peoples that understand each other very well, and have very frequent intercourse through their boards of trade, through their business men, through their commercial and financial transactions; and I have always thought that that should be taken into ac-

count. The moment you commence putting trade commissioners in the United States, with its large number of cities and its widely extended territory, you are embarking on a very large and expensive propaganda. The question is whether that is necessary or not. We do make use of the British consular agents in the various cities of the United States. We are in constant communication with them, and they with us; and they perform a very useful function in some respects where trade inquiries are necessary. We had also, during the war, to establish in Washington a special trade mission, which we called the War Trade Mission, and during the period of the war, particularly that portion of it in which the United States was engaged, when they made their great effort and found that their own resources magnificent as they were, and their productive powers great as they were, were not sufficient to give them quickly the equipment they needed, that trade mission performed a very useful service for Canada. Millions upon millions of dollars worth of contracts were, through the agency of that trade mission, procured for Canadian firms and for Canadian labour as well. I may say to my hon. friend that that mission is still at work in a somewhat modified form and, as will have been noticed, negotiations are at present going on looking towards the permanent establishment of a Canadian trade and diplomatic service, if you can call it such in Washington itself. We have also had for a year or more a publicity branch in New York. The work of this branch has had close connection with the Department of Trade and Commerce, and has had to do with replying to inquiries with reference to trade in various commodities with Canada and disseminating a great amount of information through the press, the Chambers of Commerce, and individual and corporate trading agencies. So that the United States has not been entirely neglected in that respect. It is an open question, what may be thought the best thing to do in the future, but the facts which I have outlined have to a considerable extent influenced the policy of the department. I may also take occasion to say that we are doing an unobtrusive but most important work in advertising Canada's resources, productive energy and enterprise, and actual processses of production, thriugti our moving-picture film service. During the last two years these films have been shown, I understand, to over six millions of people in the United States. The films are being shown also in England, Australia and 
New Zealand. I arranged a contract in England last year under which these films are to be shown on the theatre courses and in the film houses in Great Britain. That arrangement will be in full operation this year, and millions of people will see these pictures. Some of our films were shown at the Lyons fair last year. The city of Lyons gave us the use of the town hall, and our films were shown there every afternoon and evening of the two weeks that our exhibition was on. The hall was crowded and the showing of the films excited a great deal of interest. For instance, we have a complete set of films showing the waterpowers of Canada, developed, undeveloped, and in process of development; these create a keen interest in the minds of those who see them. One of our university professors, a member of the Research Council, took these films over to England and lectured on them in some of the cities there, creating much interest and doing much good in that way. During the Peace Conference I had these films, together with other exhibits, shown in a favourable position on the Champs Ely-sees in Paris. Besides the persons and institutions interested in them scientifically, I had the representatives of the different countries which took part in the negotiations at the Peace Conference see these films, and as a result much interest was manifested and many inquiries made with regard to the subjects of them. I have given a very imperfect sketch of this branch of our endeavour, but I am quite certain it is one of the least expensive and one of the most fruitful of the agencies which we are employing to make Canada and her resources known. I may add that we mix in with the films selected scenery, bits of the social and general life of the country so as to make the films interesting.
Are these pictures taken by the Conservation Commission or are they one of the activities of my hon. friend's department?

It is one of the activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce. If my hon. friend would take the time some day to visit the branch which carries on this work, at the corner of Wellington and Lyon streets, the officials there would he very glad to show him the films. I invite hon. members who have not already done so to visit that branch and see exactly what we are doing. We take the pictures ourselves; we develop the negatives, make the prints, and then send copies of the prints to the different countries that I have spoken

of. In the United States the exhibitions of these films costs us nothing; we simply provide the films and they are put through the different circuits without expense to us. In some respects we get a small revenue therefrom.

I was going to ask the
minister through what channels the pictures were circulated.
Through the circuits of the different film houses.
The minister says that instead of involving expense, this branch secures a revenue for the department?

The revenue at
the present time is small. But the main point is that the circulation of the films does not cost us anything. All those millions of people who see them are enabled to see them through their passing through the different circuits of those houses, and that costs us nothing at all. If we put up the right kind of films, those houses are very glad to get them. In our contract with the British firm, after certain expenses are deducted, we get a proportion of the profits, whatever they may happen to be.

I understood the minister to say that the commercial agencies in Belgium had been re-opened. I know there was before the war an office in the city of Antwerp in front of the Central station. The occupant of 'this position died immediately before the war, I think in the year 1914, and he was not replaced. Has the minister information whether a new man has been appointed in that city?

My hon. friend
must be a little mistaken. We had no office in Antwerp. Our office was at Rotterdam, and our trade commissioner at Rotterdam visited other points, including points in Belgium. He may have visited Antwerp, and he may have had an office there for an occasional visit. I am not sure about that.

There is an office at Antwerp, and the word "Canada" is in electric characters very visible every evening from all parts of the square in front of the Central station. I understood (Mr. Geleerd is the representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce at Rotterdam.

I will tell my
hon. friend just how the matter stands. Mr. Geleerd was a clerk in the office at Rotterdam; and when at the outbreak of war the commissioner himself left, Mr. Geleerd was kept there so as to keep a 120
locus in quo and to do a certain amount of work. But he was not a trade commissioner; he was a clerk in the office, and he administered so far as he could whilst the war was on. A new incumbent has been allocated to that section of country, and for the time being this central office is at Rotterdam; but he is conducting an examination in Holland and Belgium, and the report that he gives of the result of his examination will enable us to decide what we shall do in the future as regards those two countries. 1 It may be that a different locus in quo will be given to him, and it may be that we may have to have two trade commissioners, or it may be that we may have to have fine trade commissioner and and an assistant for the two countries.
Do I understand that Mr. Geleerd is not working for the department any more?
He is working for the department, but as a clerk, not as a trade commissioner.

What is Mr. Geleerd's salary? I know Mr. Geleerd personally. I was in Belgium for a number of weeks, and he is a young man of, I believe, quite considerable commercial reading; he is proficient in Dutch, French, English and German, and a good knowledge of those four languages is required for any employee at Rotterdam. I should like also to know the name of the new incumbent and his salary.

Mr. A. S. Bleak-ney is the new appointee for Rotterdam, and his salary is $3,000 with a living allowance of $500. He was appointed in March, 1920. He was trained in our department here, and he has a good knowledge of French. I do not appear to have the names and salaries of the staff, but I will get the information in regard to Mr. Geleerd for my hon. friend.

Mr. Geleerd was, as the minister says, in charge of the office during the war, and he was a very active young man who rendered numberless services, not only to myself, but to some other Canadians who were passing through on their way from Germany. I think he complained that his salary was a little small. I asked the question of him, and he thought he was not properly remunerated. He was in charge of the whole office, and I think he was performing the work in a satisfactory and gratifying manner.
Yes, so far as the work could be carried on, he was very satisfactory to the department. I will get the information for my hon. friend.
The Auditor General's Report, page Z-18, contains the name of Mr. Geleerd at Rotterdam, and his salary as acting trade commissioner for twelve months to March 31, 1919, is placed at $1,050.

I am certainly very much gratified at the information the minister has given us and what he has told us about these pictures he is sending throughout the country. We are on very important items and dealing with a very important department and a very important minister. I would suggest to him that if there is anybody around this Chamber taking films now, the minister should see that his censor does not permit such films to go out showing the present complexion of the House when so much important business is before us. I would warn him not to allow a film of the present benches, and particularly of
his own side of the House, to go abroad.

I will certainly make sure that if any film taker comes around; my hon. friend does not escape. The latter part df his remark is perhaps somewhat of a tribute to myself. Everybody thinks things are going on so well that they do not have to watch me.

The hon. member for Antig-onish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) has suggested to the minister the advisability of having trade commissioners in some cities in the United States. I agree with my hon. friend in that respect. With the business which is being done, especially by merchants of the Maritime Provinces in Boston and New York, and having regard to the increased business that could be done in the United States, I think it is very desirable that we should have agencies in that country. My information is that we really have some sort of offices in both New York and Boston. I was told a few days ago that a gentleman by the name c' Colonel Cooper was in charge of the New York office. There is also an officer, I understand, at Boston to whom we are paying the princely sum of $1,800 to look after our interests. This gentleman' complained very bitterly a few days ago that it was impossible for him to do any work on that sum. It seems to me that a man who is looking after the interests of the Canadian people in Boston is

certainly deserving of consideration, and I think he should be far better paid. If there is such a man, and any information is that there is, it is a disgrace and a shame for the Government to pay him only $1,800 a year.

So far as my
department is concerned, I have no officer in Boston and never have had. The Publicity Office in New York is not directly under my charge, but under the charge of the President of the Privy Council, I know Colonel Cooper who is in charge of the work there, and he is in constant communication with my department and contributes a large amount of valuable information on trade matters.

iSome department of the
Government keeps an officer in Boston. If he is of no use, and the Government does not know he is there, they had better withdraw him. If he is there and is doing work ,for the people of Canada and for the business .men of the Maritime Provinces especially, we should pay him a sufficient amount so that he can have a proper staff to do his work. If he is not under the Department ,of Trade and Commerce, I should like the .minister to make inquiries and find out whether this man is a Trade Commissioner or what he is.

He is not a
Trade Commissioner, but I shall be very glad to make inquiry.

In view of the very good services rendered by the gentleman I referred to a few moments ago, Mr. Geleerd, in Rotterdam, and as he is the father of a family and devotes the whole of his time to that office, performing duties which are lhore than clerical-he did during the war at all events-I would humbly suggest to the minister that he take into consideration a slight increase, say 25 per cent per annum, in the remuneration of this gentleman, as he receives only $1,000 a year.
I will take that into consideration.
What is being done to develop trade with the West Indies?

In the last ten years there has been a big development in trade with the West Indies. 1 have not the figures of the trade before me, but I remember going over them a short time ago. As the committee knows, we framed a preferential arrangement with certain of the West India Islands in 1912. That has

a currency of ten years, running out in 1022, and it has worked excellently well. It did not embrace all of the West India Islands. Jamaica did not give any preference to commercial exports from Canada although we gave to Jamaica, and have continued to do so up to the present time, the benefit of our preference to the other West India Islands. Lately it has been decided to have a conference similar to the one we had in 1912, but this time between all of the West India Islands, including Jamaica, the Bahamas, Bermuda, British Honduras, and of course Demerara. The arrangements are pretty well completed, and the date of the conference has been set for the 31st of May. On that date we hope to have a fully representative set of delegates from all of the British administrations I have mentioned.
The minister did not mention Trinidad; is that included?

Yes. We hope also to have a representative of the British Board of Trade. The subjects the conference will take up are communications, transport and cable, and trade relations, the object being to enlarge, if we possibly can, the volume of trade between us by an extension of the preference. We hope for good results from the conference.
Mr. J ,H. SINCLAIR:	Where will it be
held?
In Ottawa.
There is no regular communication with the Bahama islands, and 1 would suggest to the minister that the advisability of bettering the communication be taken up at the conference.
That is one of the subjects for discussion.
I notice we have an item of $38,933.33 for West India cable. Does the Government pay that amount towards the cable service with the West Indies?

I am very glad to hear the minister say that the cable service will be resumed, because for the last year or so it has been very unsatisfactory. Sometimes it takes as much as a week for a cable to go from Canada to the West Indies and the reply to come Oa'Uc, and (hat seriously interferes with business. It is absolutely necessary for business men that their cables shall arrive at their destinations quickly, so that they can get replies as soon as possible. Competition is keen and it is necessary to catch the steamers that are sailing between Canada and the West Indies, and sometimes the cables are only sent twenty-four hours before the steamer sails from Halifax or St. John.

What is the idea of voting this item "development and extension of Canadian trade " by itself and a little later, having an item which concludes with " other expenditur es connected with the extension of Canadian trade"? Both items appear to relate to the same subject.

They are the
same subject to some extent, but the second one has particular reference to the old service which has been carried on for a long series of years and which has been devoted

entirely to the work of the trade commis-sionerships. The different items of expenditure I read were for development alone; that line-films, exhibitions, and the like of that. In view of that there seems to be an advantage in keeping the trade commissioner-ship work by itself so that we can follow it by comparison. The other vote is allocated to the special and varied services.

Propaganda
work?
Yes, propaganda work.
Have we a commissioner in Newfoundland?
We have a commissioner in Newfoundland. He was appointed under the regime of my hon. friend, I think, and he is there yet.
We had one years ago.
Yes. At the present time he is at St. Pierre Miquelon. We sent him there to look into the possibilities of the trade which may be developed with Canada.
In connection with the Glasgow service I see there is mention made of "J. D. Lithgow, refund." I understand that Mr. Lithgow has retired from the service. Am I correct in that?

Yes, he was
superannuated.
In what particulars do the functions of the trade commissioner resemble the duties of a consul general?

They have no
diplomatic functions and they confine themselves entirely to matters of' trade. They keep in communication with different departments of the Government and they keep in direct communication with business houses through their districts. They make reports here, they furnish information in reference to Canada at the other end, and do everything possible to advance the trade of Canada in their particular districts.
Are they appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

Yes.
Honorary Advisory Council of Industrial and Scientific Research, salaries and expenses, including printing and stationery, and the collection and distribution of information, and for studentships, fellowships, special problems and forestry studies, $120,000.

with the lecommendation made last year by the Scientific Committee Research?

before that but it is in the line of the same.
Patent Record, $40,000.

Is the minister still
publishing that bulky book that we used to get from the patent office and which nobody wants?

When my hon. friend says nobody wants it, maybe we do not want it here but it seems to be an absolute necessity for those who are interested in getting out patents. The patent office is of course a paying office and the surplus over expenditure is quite large.
I am not bringing this up for the first time. It has been before the House quite frequently, and I thought that it was, if not struck out altogether, curtailed in circulation.

There has been no money as yet paid on that account. It was a contract entered into during the war when it was absolutely impossible for us to get the linen yarns and threads which were necessary for certain things in connection with fishermen's nets and manufacturing industries. We entered into a contract by which we agreed to give a certain bounty for three years on linen yarns of a certain measurement or size, according to the measurements they have as to fineness. A sum of $75,000 was set aside as the maximum which should be paid in three years. Of that, $25,000 was to be the maximum paid in one year and the subsidy was to end the third year.
Nothing -has been paid yet.

No adjustments have been made, but the industry itself was established and was carried on. It was decided that no subsidy should be paid until the war had ceased. That was based on the ground that prices were quite high

whilst the war was being carried on, but that a hard time would come when the war ceased and the war prices fell, and tihe bounty was guaranteed to them against loss. I am just now taking up the matter as to arrangements for payment. If the committee would like the item to stand, I will agree to that course and furnish the explanation later.
Weights and Measures, ?26 9,2-65.

This is a branch which has been transferred to my department in the different allocations that were given to some of the services that came from the Inland Revenue Department. It will be seen that there is a decrease from the old vote.
Gas and Electricity; salaries of inspectors and assistant inspectors of gas and electricity;- rent, fuel, travelling expenses for gas and electricity inspection, and the purchase of instruments, etc., $138,90'0.

The gas and electricity service also came to my department in the allocation of services from the Inland Revenue Department, and the vote is just about the same as last year. This is a branch which more than pays its expenses and yields a surplus. The weights and measures branch does not quite make -up its expenses; the two branches together pretty nearly do so.

When this item was before the House last year I brought to the notice of the minister who had Charge of the electricity branch, the fact that I was receiving a great many complaints, that we have no proper inspection of electric light companies, etc., in my part of the country. I forget -who was the minister to. whom I addressed myself at that time, but I remember I was promised that a better state of things would prevail. I now bring to my hon. friend's notice the fact that there is no* government inspection in eastern Nova Scotia, and ask him to see to it that the proper officer is instructed to look into- the situation in that part of the country.
If my hon. friend will give me the locality to which he refers and will let me know the facts I will have them looked into.

I refer to the three towns of Sydney, North Sydney and Sydney Mines, where the electric light companies do pretty much as they please. The electric light meters in those towns may or may not be'right but there is no government official there to establish the fact. We have had the experience of no lights being used at
all for a whole month, or perhaps two months, and yet when the bill was presented it was for as large an amount as if there had been a consumption of light all the time. There have been a great many complaints, and we would like to have some sort of effective Government control so that the companies concerned may be more careful.

Does this item apply to the inspection of the operations of companies of a provincial character? I suppose it does. I think the companies to which my hon. friend refers are the local companies, and I was wondering Whether Dominion inspection applies to them. I suppose, as this is an inspection service, it would apply to all, but I am not clear on the point.

I think the .point was raised last year when I brought the matter to the notice of the department. My recollection is that the minister then in charge of the branch said they could exercise control regardless of how the company was incorporated.

I think that is right. There is an inspection district, the central or head office being in Halifax. However, I will make inquiries and let my hon. friend know. I move that the committee rise and report progress.

Before the committee rises may I ask my hon. friend whether there was any vote taken last year under the heading of demobilization? I notice that there is a vote of $38,463,400 for this purpose on the last page of the Estimates.
I think a general vote was taken, and out of that vote allocations were made for certain classes of war expenditure which were entailed on the departments because of the Military Service Act.
I presume we will be able to get the details of that expenditure before we are asked to consider this item.
No doubt.
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.
